speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF SIXTH MEETING OF JOINT CANADA-U.S. COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to make an announcement respecting the sixth annual meeting of the joint Canada-United States committee on trade and economic affairs. This meeting will be held in Washington on March 13 and 14, as was indicated in a joint statement by the Prime Minister and President Kennedy during the former's visit to Washington on February 20.
Canada will be represented by the Minister of Finance, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, the Minister of National Revenue and the Minister of Agriculture. The United States will be represented by Hon. Dean Rusk, Secretary of State; Hon. George W. Ball, undersecretary of state for economic affairs; Hon. C. Douglas Dillon, Secretary of the Treasury; Hon. Stewart Udall, Secretary of the Interior; Hon. Orville L. Freeman, Secretary of Agriculture; and Hon. Luther H. Hodges, Secretary of Commerce.
This will be a regular meeting of this committee for the purpose of discussing economic and trade matters of mutual interest to our two countries. These meetings have proved 90205-6-178i
valuable over the years in furthering understanding between the two governments on questions affecting their economic relations.
The last meeting was held in Washington on February 16 and 17 last year. The venue for these meetings has alternated between Ottawa and Washington. However, the committee is meeting again in Washington this year in order to expedite consultation and as a matter of convenience to the new United States administration.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF SIXTH MEETING OF JOINT CANADA-U.S. COMMITTEE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as the Acting Prime Minister has said, over the years this committee has proved its usefulness, and no doubt when it meets next week it will have an opportunity to add to that usefulness because there are a great many immediately urgent questions in the economic relations between the two countries to which consideration needs to be given. I would hope that the Acting Prime Minister and the other members of the Canadian delegation to the conference will see fit to bring up such questions as tourist purchase exemptions, which are now before the United States congress and, indeed, the impact on United States-Canadian trade and economic relations of some of the new economic policies of the new United States administration.

maintopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF SIXTH MEETING OF JOINT CANADA-U.S. COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think this meeting is very much needed at this time to discuss some of the important economic problems facing our two countries. Particularly in the field of agricultural surpluses it is necessary in my opinion to have an understanding with the United States so that Canada, as well as the United States, will have the opportunity to increase its exports of agricultural products. I am also certain that on the agenda should be the question of oil exports from Canada, with the hope that we can increase our exports of oil to the United States. There are many other outstanding economic problems on which I do not need to elaborate at this time. I am hopeful that this meeting may bear fruit.

subtopic: TABLING OF REPORT "PRIVATE AND PUBLIC INVESTMENT IN CANADA  OUTLOOK 1961"

speechtext:
Hon. George H. Hees (Minister of Trade
and Commerce): Mr. Speaker, I am tabling today the report "Private and Public Investment in Canada-Outlook 1961", which summarizes the results of a recent survey of capital spending intentions. The survey, conducted annually, is designed to cover the anticipated outlays for new plant and equipment, institutional and government facilities and housing.
Capital expenditure plans for all sectors of the economy, as outlined in this report, involve total outlays in 1961 of $8,336 million. This anticipated expenditure exceeds actual outlays of last year by more than $100 million and represents a continuation of the high and relatively stable level of capital spending realized in recent years.
Within the total program, the principal increases are anticipated in institutional building and government projects. New hospital building in particular will be sharply expanded. There is also the expectation of a somewhat higher level of house building activity. On the other hand, capital outlays by business establishments on the basis of stated intentions will be a little lower than in the preceding year. This reduction reflects mainly a smaller program in the transportation industry, with requirements for both permanent facilities and equipment being

down. Outlays by commodity producing industries in total are approximately unchanged; larger expenditures related to natural gas developments are offset by reductions in certain other industries, notably iron and steel. Commercial construction for stores and office buildings is likely to continue at the high rate of 1960.
I should like to indicate also that it has been possible to include in this report a breakdown of the capital expenditure figures for provinces and major cities. In preceding years this regional material was not available until some time after the release of the national figures. The regional statistics indicate increased capital programs for 1961 in most of the provinces. In those provinces for which somewhat lower outlays are indicated, notably Manitoba and New Brunswick, unusually large expansion programs were completed last year.
The anticipated level of capital spending, if realized, will result in some net increase in demands upon the economy. An increase of 4 per cent in outlays for new construction is indicated. This will involve greater activity in the construction trades and related industries. On the other hand, the 2 per cent reduction in total outlays for machinery and equipment will affect mainly import items. Demands on domestic equipment producers should remain at about the 1960 level.
The results of the survey indicate that planned capital outlays, considered in relation to national output, will remain at a high level and will involve the continuing build-up in the capital stock of the economy.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: TABLING OF REPORT "PRIVATE AND PUBLIC INVESTMENT IN CANADA  OUTLOOK 1961"
speechtext:
It is, of course, difficult to comment on an important statement of this kind which has just been made to the house and which we have had no opportunity to study, especially since it has been made in considerable statistical detail.
The planned capital expenditures, Mr. Speaker, are an important indication each year of the prospects for the economy for the current and forthcoming year. While there has been no opportunity to study the figures given by the minister, it is quite clear from what the minister has said that the plans for capital expenditures in this country this year are not such as to take care of the increased need for employment which will undoubtedly result from the increase in the labour force of this country.

subtopic: TABLING OF REPORT "PRIVATE AND PUBLIC INVESTMENT IN CANADA  OUTLOOK 1961"
speechtext:
It is most difficult at this time to comment on the statement made by the minister without having been given any previous notice of it. I would say that I feel the statement is being made at the right time, since the labour estimates
Inquiries of the Ministry will be under discussion soon and we shall have a chance to relate the figures in this statement to the unemployment situation. As I heard the minister's statement I would say that while a small increase in capital outlay is forecast, it seems conclusive from the statement he has made that there will be no major upturn in the economy, certainly not sufficient to provide employment for those now unemployed.
We welcome the minister's statement at this time in relation to the debate about to take place, and will have further comments to make later.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: CANNED PORK
subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO TESTS OF QUALITY
speechtext: I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Agriculture, notice of which I was able to give him just a few moments age. Would the minister comment on a press report that federal government surplus canned pork being distributed in the Windsor area is unfit to eat? Has the government provided any check to test the quality of its canned pork still in storage so that its quality is assured before distribution?

subtopic: CANNED PORK
subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO TESTS OF QUALITY
speechtext:
I should like to thank the hon. member for his interest in this matter. I am informed that the canned pork in question was part of a lot of 23,370 cases released at Toronto by the stabilization board to the Ontario department of welfare on April 1, 1960. Early in January, 1961 some 3,000 cases were sent to the social service authorities in Windsor. That agency has been distributing the product to needy people.
Reports that the product was faulty have been checked by officials of my department. They were informed by the office of the Windsor medical officer of health that samples were examined by the provincial health laboratory in Windsor and that the laboratory found no evidence of anything being wrong with the product. However, in view of the incidents of yesterday I have asked my department to check more thoroughly into the procedure followed with regard to this type of distribution.
There were also reports that some of the cans were bulging. Examination of several cans indicated that any evidence of bulging was due to overfilling, but I would have the department look into this further.

subtopic: CANNED PORK
subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO TESTS OF QUALITY

subtopic: AVAILABILITY OF EMPLOYMENT RECORDS OF UNEMPLOYED PERSONS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in these main estimates the total amount requested is $136,497,933. The Department of Labour is asking for the sum of $33,879,953 and the unemployment insurance commission for $102,617,980. Of the $33,879,953 for the Department of Labour, $26,600,000 is required to carry out the purposes of the Technical and Vocational Training Assistance Act. This represents an increase of over $17 million in the amount provided for this program in 1960-61.
Honourable members will recall that when the new bill to expand technical and vocational training in Canada was introduced last November I spoke of the many compelling reasons for increased training in Canada. I should like to bring to the attention of the committee the fact that notwithstanding this

Supply-Labour
substantial increase in our vocational training program, page 39 of the blue book shows a decrease of slightly over $12 million in the department's estimates from that which was voted in 1960-61. I should also explain that in the 1960-61 estimates column there is an item of $30 million which was voted for the municipal winter works incentive program, and there is no comparable figure in the 1961-62 column.
I wish to assure the committee at this point that this municipal winter works incentive program will be continued during the winter of 1961-62 should the extent of seasonal unemployment warrant it and should the government decide to do so. Moneys required for this purpose will be included in a later supplementary departmental estimate.
The other increases in the operational votes are generally speaking in the salary allotments, and are largely due to the general salary increases which were given to civil servants and authorized by the government last summer.
I should now like to deal generally with the main activities of the Department of Labour. When presenting my departmental estimates it has been my usual practice to speak briefly on the various functions of the department. My remarks will concern the highlights of activities which give rise to the financial requirements over the coming fiscal year.
First, we give every assistance possible to labour and management in developing constructive relationships and in improving the skills of the work force. Second, we assist in bringing into employment and training those who are unemployed. I assure you, Mr. Chairman, that in the campaign against unemployment we are mobilizing and will continue to mobilize all the resources at the disposal of the federal government. The points I wish to make today in assisting hon. members in their consideration of my department's estimates concern the programs of the various branches of my department and the positive contribution they make every day to improving the welfare of Canadians.
Today's manpower problems have established the changing and expanding work of my department. We have expanded and greatly intensified our work in those activities most directly concerned with dealing with unemployment through creating job opportunities and developing the skills of the labour force. For example, the experience of the first two years of our municipal winter works incentive program demonstrated to us that this program could create winter jobs. On the basis of this experience we greatly expanded the scope of the program and its duration, and as a result, Mr. Chairman,

almost twice the number of direct jobs have been created through the program this year. We know that methods of construction and programming of work which were available before the start of our "do it now" program, but not used to any great extent, have become a well known and accepted part of Canadian life and this to me, Mr. Chairman, spells success.
We have found that a wide gap exists in the contribution of vocational training to the development of the skills and the requirements of Canadian industry. I have already mentioned the substantial increase in the amounts we are asking to be voted for this program during the coming year. The increase in our expenditures in support of vocational training programs from $9,197,600 a year ago to $26,600,000 for the fiscal year 1961-62 stems largely from the positive action taken by this government to provide facilities and programs to meet the requirements of industry and workers in such training.
I refer to the Technical and Vocational Training Assistance Act which received royal assent last December. Already the effect of this new legislation, with its realistic approach to the problems of training for trades and technical skills at all levels, are being felt. Financial impediments to the development of adequate training facilities have been removed. From the Atlantic provinces to the west coast important expansions are under way or about to begin. For example, at St. John's, Newfoundland, a new college of trade and technical training is being built at a cost initially estimated at more than $4 million. Nova Scotia has forecast the construction of a provincial trade school and a vocational high school. The province of New Brunswick is proceeding with the construction of a provincial technical institute and is planning three additional trade schools. Ontario's plans have not as yet been announced but very much expanded facilities are in prospect. Prince Edward Island is advancing plans for the construction of training facilities at a new centre, and we have received assurances that the province of Quebec will enter into an agreement with the federal government under the new act and will implement plans already made for construction of new facilities and expansions of many which are already in use. Manitoba is planning a combined institute of technology and a trade school at an estimated cost of $5 million. Alberta and British Columbia each have plans well under way for extensive capital projects.
This rapid development in, capital expenditure programs represents a response by the provinces to the federal government offer made in this new legislation to assume

75 per cent of the capital costs of new facilities incurred up to March 31, 1963. More and better training facilities are needed and it appears, Mr. Chairman, that we are going to have them.
The cost of federal sharing in these capital developments during the fiscal year 1961-62 is estimated at $14,175,000, exclusive of Quebec. If Quebec completes an agreement this amount will undoubtedly be higher. In some cases facilities to accommodate additional trainees will be ready for use within the new fiscal year. Other projects while taking longer to complete, will provide early relief to our urgent training needs.
Immediate increases in the, sharing of provincial expenditures for the operation of technical and vocational schools are promoting an immediate expansion of training enrolments to the limit of facilities currently available. In our estimates for the coming year we have provided $4 million for the training of unemployed workers compared with $1,310,000 for the fiscal year 1960-61. In 1960 the federal government offered to share with the provinces to the extent of 75 per cent of the cost of this training, once a minimum level of training had been reached. The program has gained momentum rapidly. In the fiscal year 1959-60 some 3,600 unemployed persons had been given training to January 31, 1960. By the same date in the fiscal year 1960-61 more than 7,000 had been given training. For the months of February and March marked increases in enrolments are expected as the provincial programs gain momentum. Training classes have been established in 385 centres in a total of 82 different occupations, and as additional facilities become available we expect to have a program extensive enough to cover all unemployed persons who can profit by training.
The program for training indentured apprentices is also continuing to grow. By the end of January in the fiscal year 1959-60 there had been just short of 10,000 new enrolments for apprenticeship. By January 31 this year there had been more than 11,100 new enrolments. The continued expansion of facilities for this training will provide for further increases in the coming year.
The foregoing are the largest items of expenditure for which we have budgeted in our estimates to cover the technical and vocational training program. The program of training of disabled persons, an effective means to restore handicapped workers to active careers of self-support, is continuing to grow, with a vote of $370,000 as the federal share of the program. Other programs for training in primary industries, as foremen and
Supply-Labour
supervisors, for student aid and vocational correspondence courses will continue. An expanded program of assistance to students attending post-high school courses in science and technology below university level has been introduced. The need for technicians and other skilled workers at a level between that of the tradesman and the professional man has become acute in industry. It must be satisfied, Mr. Chairman, if our economy is to keep abreast of world competition.
A new program of assistance to persons training as technical and vocational teachers, supervisors and administrators is being developed. Too frequently our technical and vocational institutions have had extreme difficulty in recruiting competent staffs. Many Canadians wishing to prepare for careers in this field have had to seek their training in the United States or elsewhere. The expected growth in our vocational institutions will create additional and urgent staffing problems.
I had occasion recently to meet with representatives of the provinces at a conference called to discuss proposals for a new federal-provincial agreement to implement the provisions of the new Technical and Vocational Training Assistance Act, and their response to the possibilities opened by the new act was most gratifying to me. The provisions of the agreements to be made under it and the programs authorized were generally acceptable. There appeared to be an air of satisfaction and eagerness on the part of all provincial representatives to get ahead with the training program which the new look in our legislation has made possible.
We are constantly developing our understanding of employment and unemployment and the more effective utilization of our manpower resources through the work of the economics and research branch. One of the principal functions of the branch is the continuing analysis of labour market conditions and the examination of the meaning of trends and events in labour markets for the demand and supply of labour. The value of this information is self-evident. Publication of a good deal of this information has proved of value to parliament, labour and management, provincial governments and the public at large.
Continuing work on the character of our manpower resources and their participation within the Canadian economy has facilitated a deeper understanding of the character of our employment and unemployment problems. For example, the publication this year of studies of seasonal employment and unemployment has made available to us new insights into the nature of this problem. It has strengthened the government's view that

Supply-Labour
much can be done through the winter works program to provide employment for those who find themselves unemployed during the winter months.
The branch has also participated in joint studies with the provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick for the purpose of examining the problems of seasonal unemployment in those provinces. These studies will reinforce other work going on in the branch concerning the nature of workers who are not able to secure continuing employment.
The field of manpower training is one to which much research has been devoted over the past several years, and this work has helped to shape the character of our new legislation on training. This work has involved a detailed investigation of shifting occupational and industrial needs within the labour force and of the required technical qualifications. Studies have been carried out on the effects of automation on manpower in specific industries and on the evaluation of a wide range of technological changes on manpower requirements. In the field of professional personnel, further work has been undertaken to determine the nature of supply and demand trends, particularly for scientists and engineers. One important aspect, Mr. Chairman, of the employment of workers is covered by the continuing work of the economics and research branch in the labour management field. Similarly, in today's world, the branch is investigating the important problem of the costs of fringe benefits and the significance of labour costs on the whole Canadian economy.
The regular work of the branch in connection with wages, working conditions and collective bargaining has continued, and publications have been issued on a regular basis. In addition to the general work in the field of employment and unemployment, there is provision in the work of the department for continuing programs in a number of important areas. I shall refer here, Mr. Chairman, to only four of these fields. Our women's bureau works closely with the national employment service and other groups in developing an understanding of the problems of women in the labour force and for the promotion of good employment standards for women. Through the special services branch, programs are administered in the farm labour field and in connection with the organized movement of workers between Canada and the United States.
The civilian rehabilitation branch, in cooperation with the Department of National Health and Welfare, the unemployment insurance commission and the vocational training branch, continues to co-ordinate at the federal level all these services that contribute
to the vocational rehabilitation of disabled persons. It is assisting the provinces to organize programs or endeavours to bring together in an organized pattern all government and voluntary efforts that seek to remove the disadvantages experienced by so many of our handicapped citizens. The value of this program, Mr. Chairman, has been clearly established and, on the basis of provincial needs, we are asking for increased provincial support in this area of activity.
A division of older workers has been established within the civil rehabilitation branch. Through these efforts and the efforts of the unemployment insurance commission, we see evidence that many more of our employers are realizing the valuable contributions that the experience and maturity of the older worker can make. I have taken a very personal interest in the employment problems of older people in a variety of ways, and I am most encouraged by the response of employers to our efforts in this field.
The special services branch of the department co-ordinates our many significant activities in the field of winter employment. These include the winter employment program and the municipal winter works incentive program. Both these programs have grown out of a conviction on our part, through research in the seasonal unemployment problems of the Canadian economy, that a great deal can be done to develop employment during the winter months. The winter employment program, jointly administered by the Department of Labour and the unemployment insurance commission, has become the focus of national interest. It enlists the support of national and local organizations, of industry, of labour and of every available publicity medium in stimulating winter employment.
An example here, Mr. Chairman, has been set by federal government departments and agencies in carrying out maximum construction, maintenance, repairs and purchasing during the winter months. Public spirited citizens in the towns and cities from coast to coast deserve great credit for the time and effort they put in each fall and winter on behalf of the local "do it now" campaigns. Organizations, such as the Canadian Construction Association, the Canadian Manufacturers' Association and other nationally known organizations are taking an active interest in the stimulation of winter employment and are intensifying their efforts each year. National advertising is contributing hundreds of thousands of dollars worth of public service support on behalf of the winter employment campaign.
We have found, Mr. Chairman, that for every dollar spent by the government more

than $10 is spent by business and other groups on advertising and publicity to increase winter employment. This year's municipal winter works incentive program was enthusiastically promoted by provincial governments and municipalities across the country. Over 5,900 projects submitted by 1,820 municipalities and 44 Indian bands have been accepted. This program may be compared with the 2,600 projects previously undertaken by 861 municipalities during the winter of 1959-60.

Applications under this program are still coming in from the municipalities at the rate of over 100 per week.
A variety of other activities of the Department of Labour have continued. For example, the department has provided leadership in Canada's work within the international labour organization. During 1960 Canada was represented at seven international labour organization meetings by tripartite delegations. Similar meetings are scheduled for 1961 including, for the first time in five years, an international labour organization American regional conference to which we will be sending a delegation.
The department undertakes a number of diverse activities which, in one measure or another, support the department's work as a whole. In today's world, where pensions have become the rule rather than the exception, we are sometimes inclined to underrate the value of the annuities program which also comes under my department. Individuals, not
Supply-Labour
able through their employment to secure pensions, are assumed of low cost annuity plans. The group contracts by our annuities branch have also provided an effective and secure means of investment for employees in various industries across the country.
The annuities branch sells individual annuities, both deferred and immediate, and group annuities. At the close of the last fiscal year there were in force 116,057 individual deferred annuity contracts and 231,424 certificates for employees in group pension plans. In addition, annuities were being paid under 818,228 matured contracts and certificates at the rate of $43,403,649 a year. The net premium income for the fiscal year 1959-60 was $56,041,417, and the annuities account in the consolidated revenue fund totalled over $1,100 million as at March 31, 1960.
The industrial relations branch of the department is responsible for the administration of the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act, the Fair Employment Practices Act, the Annual Vacations with Pay Act, the Fair Wages and Hours of Labour Act and the promotion of labour-management committees in industry.
The function of the Department of Labour which has the longest history lies, of course, in the field of industrial relations. The Canada Fair Employment Practices Act continues to be a most effective weapon in the struggle against discrimination in employment. My department believes that not one application for employment form coming within federal jurisdiction contains questions contrary to the provisions of the act, though at the time of the passage of the bill the great majority of employers' application forms contained questions asking the prospective employee his race, religion, national origin or colour.
The labour-management co-operation service has continued to stimulate the development of labour-management committees in Canadian industry. Today there are in excess of 1,600 committees in industry across the country. The complex nature of our industrial relations system in Canada, the importance of many industrial disputes both to the country as a whole and to the thousands of individual workers and employers affected, is obvious. The responsibilities of labour and management to work together in securing the greatest possible benefit for their joint endeavours is great, and rests squarely on the shoulders of labour and management.

As usual, then, the hon. member was out of order. Sometimes the gulf which appears to divide labour and management in this country seems difficult to bridge. It must be bridged. I have asked labour and management groups to meet and address themselves to problems of higher productivity, of technological change, and the whole field of joint interests. In this direction, I say, lies the solution to many of our contentious problems. Since we felt that an effort on our part could bring them together, the Minister of Trade and Commerce and I have asked representatives of industry and labour to meet here in Ottawa on March 15. We are sending out that invitation in the hope that we can create an atmosphere in which both labour and management can resolve the difficulties which they have faced and are facing.
I should like to say something now about the operations of the unemployment insurance commission, which administers the national employment service and unemployment insurance. As hon. members are aware, these operations are receiving a good deal of attention from both the government and the public; rightly so, since they are vital to the well-being of so many of our citizens at this time as well as to the prosperity of our country as a whole. This prosperity will be secured only through long range positive

action, and it is in line with this conviction that the employment side of the commission's work has been consistently improved, especially of late. It is of the utmost importance that unemployed persons be placed in jobs with the least delay. It is equally important that such placements should be satisfactory not only to the workers concerned but also to their employers and to other workers.
In carrying out this program, officers of the service made more than a quarter of a million visits to employers last year in order to explain the facilities of the national employment service and to obtain orders for workers. In another direction, the employment service is constantly seeking out applicants with the skills required to meet employers' orders which cannot readily be filled from applications on file. As I advised the committee during the last debate on these estimates, steps were being taken at that time to strengthen the employment service staff, and these endeavours are already bearing fruit. We are thus engaged in an effort to improve the quality of the service and also to improve the use of the service by the public through a public relations program.
I am happy to say that this two-pronged approach, although of comparatively recent origin, has already produced results both tangible and intangible, particularly when measured against current economic factors. Thus, although placements for the calendar year 1960 were 2.8 per cent lower than they were for 1959, the last three months for which placement figures are available-* November, December and January-show an increase of 16.7 per cent compared with the corresponding period of 1959-60.
During 1960 the employment service placed 950,300 persons in jobs and it is noteworthy, I think, that of this number of placements 120,134 were workers aged 45 and over. This has been brought about in part as a result of the older workers program in which I am particularly interested, and it emphasizes again the value of public information to which reference was made earlier. During the past year 300 employers employing some 60,000 workers have either raised the age limit specified on their hiring applications or removed it entirely.
Another direction in which progress has been made is the placement service to youth, including career counselling for young people in school or just entering the labour market. I may say that a considerable number of school drop-outs returned to school as a result of national employment service counselling.
Among the special services given by the commission are those for the physically handicapped and veterans, placement service

to young Indians as part of their integration into urban life, to immigrant workers, and so forth. A sharp intensification of interest in vocational training has brought about many more directions of unemployed workers to courses of training by national employment service officers than ever before.
Taken separately, these things are of more immediate concern to some groups of citizens than to others. In their total effect, however, they are of fundamental importance for the Caandian economy as a whole. The commission believes, and I share this relief, that better placements will not only lead to better production but will also lead to the employment of more workers.
Hon. members will be interested to note that the commission's efforts to safeguard the fund against improper claims have been stepped up through a strengthening of the investigation division and an educational program. It is of course unavoidable that unlawful practices in the use of unemployment insurance stamps and in claims for benefit will crop up either as single incidents or as a rash of incidents. It is therefore necessary that the insurance provisions of the act, such as those relating to insurability, contract of service, availability for work and so on, be enforced and explained with both perseverance and understanding. As a result of the efforts on the part of the enlarged investigation division, the number of detected punishable infractions of the act rose from 17,279 in 1959 to 29,619 in 1960.
The commission's audit division, whose task is checking to ensure that employers comply with the act, completed 189,068 audits during 1960 and made 38,417 investigations, both figures being slightly higher than those for 1959. The number of registered employers in Canada subject to audit rose to 382,879, an increase of over 9,000 compared with the previous year.
The total amount required for the unemployment insurance commission is $102,617,980. This of course includes the government's contribution to the unemployment insurance fund of $57 million. The net increase in the commission's administrative costs is some $5,155,000. This increase is due primarily to salary increases and to an increase in personnel, notably in the investigation division.
Before concluding, Mr. Chairman, I wish to say something further about unemployment. This is, of course, one of the serious problems with which we have to deal at the present time. Hon. members are familiar with the fact that in a matter of months-as a matter of fact since November 17, 1960-this government has brought forward a wide range of positive and constructive measures to deal with the social

blight of unemployment and to give an upward push to our economy. I have every confidence that the actions we have taken will produce the desired results and will have the desired effect. Unemployment is not something which can cure itself. It can only be cured and its consequences arrested by a massive attack across the whole field of the general economy-

Mr. Chairman, in opening my remarks on the work of the minister's department and the problems that face that department I should like to begin by paying a tribute to the efficient and selfless work of the members of the Department of Labour from the deputy minister down.
Perhaps I could say a special word about the deputy minister who retired this year, Mr. Arthur Brown. I confess that I am prejudiced very much in his favour. He and I entered university together at a very young age; we went to war together; we came back about the same time; we came to Ottawa about the same time, and I know something about the work he has done to serve his country over the years, and is still doing in another capacity after retirement from the public service of Canada. In wishing him well I should like to associate the members of this party with the good wishes that I am also extending to his successor, Mr. George Haythorne.
As I have a great deal to say that will be critical of the policy of the minister, perhaps I should say at the beginning that I, as do all hon. members on this side, respect his sincerity and his willingness to help us when we ask him questions. We also appreciate the important and complex problems with which he is faced as Minister of Labour.
Mr. Chairman, the discussion on item 1 of the estimates of the Department of Labour provides an opportunity to review the work of the department as well as to initiate a discussion of the problems that face it. The minister has given us the first, a review of the activities of his department, for which we are grateful, but he has dealt in an almost ludicrously inadequate way with the problems which face the department, and above all, with the problem of unemployment in this country to which he devoted two or three minutes at the end of his fairly long statement.
The minister explained in doing so that this was not a matter with which he felt it necessary to deal on item 1 of his estimates. The inadequacy of the minister's statement in this regard, especially in respect of unemployment, is discouraging and disheartening. You would have thought, that he

was making a routine report regarding the activities of the Department of Labour during a normal year of full employment in this country instead of during a year when, in January, 11 per cent of the working force was unemployed.
In the face of that situation the minister did say that unemployment was one of the serious problems with which we have to deal. He also said that the government had mobilized all the resources of the federal government to deal with this problem. The result of that mobilization is reflected by the figure for unemployment that we received in January and will be reflected by the figure for February which we will be receiving within a few days.
The minister has given no indication this afternoon of the seriousness of this problem. He has not attempted to analyse the problem of unemployment. He has not put forward any new ways or means to deal with it. He has given us no policy statement at all regarding this matter. I urge the minister to rectify this omission before this item passes.
So far as I am concerned this afternoon, Mr. Chairman, my intervention at this point of our discussion is to address certain questions to the Minister of Labour in an attempt to bring out certain problems, as we on this side see them, with which we feel the government should be dealing. I intend to present our own analysis of the situation based on information we have received regarding unemployment and to ask the minister whether this analysis is sound and whether the information we bring forward to support this analysis is accurate. If the minister tells us that we are wrong in this regard we will ask him where we are wrong. I will mention some of these questions now which I intend to ask and which I hope the minister will deal with later.
The first question has regard to the rapid depletion of the unemployment insurance fund, in the face of mounting unemployment. I will ask the minister whether he agrees that the investment policy of the unemployment insurance committee by which the fund, through conversion of its victory bonds, has already been depleted by $30 million, and perhaps will be depleted to the extent of $70 million. I will ask the minister how he is going to explain this depletion to the other contributors to the fund, industry and labour.
My next question arose earlier in today's sitting and has regard to the government's intention to bring forth legislation to replenish the fund. This intention was announced by the government last November. I will ask the minister why nothing has been done in

this regard since that time. I ask the minister when it is intended that action be taken in the face of this alarming situation. The government must have been aware for more than a year that legislation of this kind was necessary. So I ask the minister to give us a reason for the delay in taking action because the committee will soon have to unload more of its bonds and thereby incur further losses.
The next question I wanted to ask-and the minister has mentioned it in his statement-concerns the alleged irregularities connected with unemployment benefits and the alleged inadequacy of the national employment service. A great deal in this regard has been read into a memorandum submitted to the Senate committee on manpower and unemployment by Dr. James. In the discussion of this matter before this committee of the other place one of the senators-a long time supporter of the Conservative party- made certain statements. I will quote from the Senate committee reports of February 2 at page 461. This senator is reported as follows:
May I suggest to you that if we were to speak about abolishing unemployment insurance entirely the unemployed would disappear by half as a good many of them have no wish to continue working steadily as long as this unemployment insurance is available for working part time.
That is an astonishing statement to appear on the records of a committee of the parliament of Canada. Even this afternoon, Mr. Chairman, we heard supporters of the government refer to widespread abuse of the unemployment insurance fund. The inference that is being drawn, and the impression that is being created throughout this country, is that hundreds of thousands of workers are cheating in regard to unemployment insurance benefits. This is a very serious impression. to create and I am sure it has no foundation in fact. I ask the minister to say something about these reflections on the efficiency of the national employment commission and the honesty of the workers of Canada. If there is something seriously wrong, can the minister inform us what is going to be done to correct it, and to strengthen and add to the efficiency of the national employment service?
The third question to which I wish to refer deals with vocational training programs. The minister did have a good deal to say about this subject. He finally recognized last December that this program and its administrative operations needed to be improved. We on this side have been pressing for that improvement since 1958. We would like to know a little more about the program. The minister gave us some information this afternoon, but we would like to know if the
Supply-Labour
minister is satisfied with the present administrative setup of the department in connection with the operation of this enlarged program. We on this side feel that a small branch in the department and an advisory council, however efficient, are not adequate to deal with this vitally important matter of vocational training.
There is another question on which the minister merely touched in his statement, namely the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act. As far back as 1958 the minister admitted that this act required amendment and change. On August 15, 1958, as reported at page 3593 of Hansard he had this to say:
Coming to the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act, may I say that I have given notice of my readiness to consider amendments to this act and that a number of suggestions have been received and are being considered at the moment.
I am still waiting for three major national organizations which have been requested to submit their recommendations, but to date I have not received them. However, on checking into the matter I find that they are in the process of completing their recommendations, and that they should be within my hands within the next few weeks.
That was August 15, 1958, but nothing has been done to carry out the intention of the minister. Since that time we have had merely postponement and delay. I ask the minister whether he still thinks this act should be improved and, if so, how does he explain the long delay in bringing forward amendments to it? Is he still waiting for the representations he expected in 1958, or has he merely shelved the whole matter? If he has not, when does he intend to introduce the amendments which he considered so desirable in 1958?
I now come to the most important of all domestic problems facing us at the present time, and one which is of particular interest and concern to the Minister of Labour who has a special responsibility for dealing with it. I refer, of course, to the question of unemployment. So far in this house, Mr. Chairman, we have been unable to get in this session or, indeed, in the previous session anything but superficial treatment by spokesmen of the government of the nature of the unemployment crisis that faces us; and of what can in fact be done about it. We on this side will keep pounding away at the seriousness of the problem even though this is subject to the cheap and tawdry response that we are prophets of doom and gloom, a reaction which we can characterize only as one of desperation on the part of the government spokesmen, a reaction on the part of hon. members in this house who in previous years on this side and in situations that

Supply-Labour
were not nearly as dangerous as they are today, in terms of unemployment did not hesitate to use much stronger language in attacking the government of that day.
At this point may I quote from an editorial in the Montreal Gazette of February 28, a paper not notoriously friendly to the Liberal party, which reads:
Just to hope that all will be well, and to refuse to mention that anything has gone wrong, may help a little, by creating an atmosphere of optimism. But it will never correct the underlying causes of what has gone wrong.
It is not being neurotic to recognize that times have changed. No one is neurotic if he faces reality and seeks a constructive adjustment to it.
This is something which has not yet happened. A well known United States commentator, Mr. Walter Lippmann, put the same point in his column on March 4, which appeared in the Ottawa Journal, when he was dealing with the fact that people who try to uncover these difficulties and underline the seriousness of the situation are open to this kind of cheap criticism which I have mentioned, and he went on to say:
They-
That is, the criticisms.
-will be unwelcome to many. They will be unwelcome to those who take the view that with words of confidence and optimism a recession like this one can be talked away-
He is not afraid to use the word "recession". I continue:
-and that the sombre truths should be glossed over and suppressed. There is everything to be said for keeping up the confidence of a sick patient. But an essential ingredient of that confidence is that the doctor is not deceiving himself. If, as seems so probable, we face a long hard effort to revive the American economy, the confidence of the people will best be sustained by convincing them that the economic doctors are not treating nice words as a substitute for real action.
Nice words, whether in Ottawa or in London, by Canadian leaders, are no substitute, and have never been a substitute, for real action. What Mr. Lippmann said in this regard about the United States has even greater application to Canada because relatively our situation is worse than that of the United States. Indeed, Mr. Coyne, the governor of the Bank of Canada, speaking in New York either yesterday or the day before-and it was a very interesting speech indeed-had this to say to his United States audience:
Trends in the growth of national product, employment and unemployment, are rather less satisfactory in Canada than in the United States. Even disregarding the population factor, for the last four or five years gross national product has improved less in Canada than in the United States.
What, then, is the situation which I have described as serious for this country? In his statement today the Minister of Labour gave us no new reason for confidence that he is
aware of what is happening to our economy, or that there has been any great departure from the position taken by the government in previous debates in this house on this subject that all we have to do is to be optimistic and all will be well; just wait. It is up to business and to labour, or even up to Mr. Kennedy. Our criticism of the government's ignorance of the underlying seriousness of this problem is, as I have said, not modified by anything that the minister has said or has not said this afternoon.
The minister did mention as an important contribution to the knowledge and understanding of the problem the proceedings of the committee of the other place on manpower and employment. Indeed, that committee is doing a most valuable work. It will be recalled that at the very beginning of the last session and the session before that we pleaded with the government to set up that kind of committee in the House of Commons so that the members of this house could participate in that kind of investigation and analysis and call before them the experts to explain the situation as they saw it.
The committee will recall that every time we tried to get this kind of investigation established in the House of Commons we were turned down. Even when we tried to persuade the government to associate the House of Commons with the investigation which had been set up through the Liberal majority in another place, we were unable to persuade the government to let us participate in what has turned out to be a most constructive and important work. It is largely on the basis of the reports before that committee that I have drawn my own conclusions of the seriousness of the trends in the economy in this country. When I talk about them, when I use the word "seriousness", I do not want anyone to think that this country will not eventually face up to and overcome those problems and once again remove that seriousness through expansion and growth. We have met very difficult and dangerous economic and employment problems before in this country and have overcome them, and we will overcome this one. But we will not do that in the way it should be done and in the time it should be done without strong, effective leadership and sound and strong policies.
Let us look at the situation, which was not explained to us by the minister at least on this occasion. We hope he may do so later. The figure I am about to give are all bureau of statistics figures which were used in reports made to the committee on employment in the other place. In the period from 1950 to 1960 there was a net increase in the labour force in this country of 1,230,000. That was accounted for to a very considerable extent by

additional female labour, particularly married women, coming into the labour force, also by men under 20 and, of course, by new immigrants to Canada.
While the labour force increased by that amount during that ten-year period, the farm labour force decreased by 340,000 which threw a greater burden on industry to supply jobs to take care of this labour force increase. Yet during that period the number of persons with jobs in this country increased by only 992,000. There is the explanation for unemployment.
If we extend the trend of the last ten years forward over the next five years, as was done in the report to the committee of the other place by Mr. Denton, an economist, and if we take a low figure for increase through immigration during the next five years-he took a figure of 100,000 per year-with the present average unemployment to be absorbed during that five years we will need 1,020,000 nonagricultural jobs to take care of our growing labour force and our present unemployment.
Are we getting these jobs? Government spokesmen say, "Oh, yes, we are getting them because employment is higher now than it has ever been in our history". They quote figures every time they speak on this subject to show that the number of people employed in the country is higher than ever before and that, of course, is quite true. However, the significant factor is not the number of employed but whether the employed are increasing at a rate sufficient to take care of the increasing labour force. If that is not happening then we get more unemployed. This increase is not taking place.
In January, 1961, it is true there were 47,000 more jobs than a year earlier. That is an increase of less than 1 per cent while during the same period unemployment increased by more than 26 per cent. As we are not getting the jobs to take care of the increase in the labour force the result, inevitably and obviously, is an increase in the percentage of unemployment. Until the economy expands so that this increase in the labour force can be taken care of the unemployment problem will be with us in the serious way in which it is today. Perhaps the figures will decrease. We hope they will, and they ought to go down in the summer. However, as I have tried to show by averaging these figures over the years, we are going to be living with this problem for some time unless there is a decided expansion in our economy.
We have had four periods of what I might perhaps call abnormal unemployment and recession since 1947, the period of 1949-50, the period of 1954-55-I am taking two during the time when my hon. friend and his party
Supply-Labour
had no responsibility for government-the period of 1957-58 and the present period from the summer of 1960 to where we are in 1961. In an analysis of these four periods of what one might call recession in the economy since the war the most striking feature is that in each successive slow-down, and we have had four, the rate of unemployment has risen higher than in the previous period and in each period of recovery we have had the rate of unemployment has fallen less.
There are three peak unemployment years, 1950, 1954 and 1958, and I think the statistics for those years will support what I have just said. In 1950 the average rate of unemployment was 3.6, in 1954 it was 4.6, in 1958 it was 7.1 and in 1960 it was just about 7 per cent. In the recovery year of 1951 unemployment fell to 2.4. In the recovery year of 1956 it fell to 3.4. In the recovery year of 1959 it feel only to 6 per cent. In January, 1961, a recession year again, the rate had reached about 11 per cent.
This indicates, I think, the validity, and importance, of an article which I read just a few hours ago during the lunch hour in the current issue of Life magazine by Dr. Heller, president Kennedy's chief economic advisor and chairman of the council of economic advisors in Washington. He is a very well known economist indeed. What he had to say on this particular point, is just as applicable, if not more so, to Canada than it is to the United States.
The economy has not been taking up the slack alter its periodic slumps and, going deeper, there is a disturbing slow-down in our rate of economic growth. The intervals between our recessions have been steadily shrinking. The up-turns have not regained the ground lost by the recession. The unemployment figures make this painfully clear.
They also make it painfully clear for Canada as well as for the United States; so clear that at the present time we have the highest percentage of unemployment in this country for 20 years and, I am informed, the highest in any industrialized free country in the western world. That, Mr. Chairman, is something to worry about.
This problem would be serious enough if it were evenly national in its impact but it is made more serious by its regional incidence, something which has been characteristic of our country ever since our country was born. The rates of unemployment are much higher in some parts of our country than they are in others. That gives us a regional problem to deal with as well as a national problem. The average in 1960 in the Atlantic provinces was 9.4 per cent and the average in Quebec was 8.5 per cent while the figures were much lower in the prairies and in Ontario.

Supply-Labour
All this shows, Mr. Chairman, that we have with us a persistent, deep-rooted problem which has, of course, no single cause and which will be susceptible to no single treatment. It is deep-rooted, it is chronic, it is regional and it is seasonal. The nature of the unemployment also adds to its complexity. A study that has been made-I confess this was a surprise to me-shows that the greatest extent of unemployment is now among young people under 20 years of age and the least extent is among women where the over-all rate of unemployment is less than half the male rate. Figures from the bureau of statistics show that whereas the average rate in 1960 was 7.3 for all ages, for women it was 3.3 and for men under 20 it was 15.6. As the minister mentioned this afternoon in his statement when dealing with vocational training, these figures emphasize the importance of vocational training and the strong relationship of education to unemployment.
A dominion bureau of statistics survey, taking the week of February 20, 1960, shows that of the people out of work 19 per cent had not completed their primary school education but only 3 per cent had completed their secondary school education. The gap, therefore, is from 19 per cent to 3 per cent.
In reporting to the employment committee of the other place, Mr. Denton summarized the situation as follows. I think this is a very good paragraph:
In summary, then, the rates of unemployment have shown a tendency to Increase with each successive recession since the war. In particular, the rates have been substantially higher for men than for women, and have consistently been highest among young people, the unskilled, and the less educated. The service producing industries have continued throughout the post-war period to provide rapidly expanding opportunities for employment, but in recent years the opportunities available in the goods producing industries have actually contracted. These changes reflect some of the basic forces which are operating in our economy.
This quotation reminds us of another very significant factor, the nature of not only unemployment but of employment in our economy today. This nature has changed considerably over the years, as the figures show. In 1950, the goods producing industries of this country were responsible for 58 per cent of the employment, whereas in 1959 they were responsible for only 48 per cent of the employment. In that category of the goods producing industries, agriculture was responsible for 20.4 per cent of the employment in 1950 and only 11.8 per cent in 1959. Manufacturing industries were responsible for 26.6 per cent of the employment in 1950 but by 1959 the figure had gone down to 25 per cent, not quite holding their own.

We know that nothing took up this slack completely, but what helped to take up some of the slack? The service industries provided 42 per cent of the employment in 1950 and 51.7 per cent of the employment in 1959. This explains among other things the increase in the number of jobs for women and the decrease in the number of jobs for men. Those manufacturing industries which are declining most in terms of employment such as gold mining, coal mining, motor parts manufacturers, farm implements, textiles and leather manufactures, are those which traditionally have employed men for the most part. All this helps to explain the nature and the seriousness of the problem that faces us. The basic reason for it, as I have already said, is a decline in the expansion of our economy. It has now reached a position of stagnation.
This afternoon, the Minister of Trade and Commerce produced a statement on private and public investment in Canada, the outlook for 1961. He gave the most optimistic interpretation possible to that statement. Since he had not sent me a copy of it in advance, it was only after I secured a copy of the press release that I had an opportunity to study it. I have had some chance to look at it while I have been in the chamber. It does not give any ground for encouragement that the situation which I have mentioned is going to be substantially corrected in the year ahead.
In so far as this particular report is concerned the minister said that, for 1961, it represents a continuation of the high and relatively stable level of capital spending realized in recent years. Well, I have just one or two comments to make on that. The proposed increase, if it is realized, will be only 1.6 per cent over 1960, and that is much too low to provide the job opportunities required by even the normal increase in our labour force let alone the high number of unemployed we have at the present time.
According to the minister's statement this afternoon, the proposed expenditures in 1961 amount to $8,330 million. This amount will actually be lower than the amount spent in 1957, 1958 or 1959 and, if expressed in constant dollars, the proposed expenditures will probably be lower than in 1960. Therefore, the declining trend which has been persistent since 1957 will unfortunately, in the light of this report, likely be continued. The report also shows that investment in business capital will be lower in 1961 than in 1960, but will be compensated by higher expenditures in the field of social capital. This does indicate the continued underlying weakness of the private sector of our economy. I hope that the forecast which we got this afternoon will not prove to be as wrong as the one that was made last year by the Minister of Trade and

Commerce. Last year the proposed expenditures were estimated by the minister at $8.77 billion, but we now see from the statement that the realized expenditures were only $8.2 billion. Instead of the forecast increase of about 4 per cent in 1960 as compared with 1959, we had a decline in 1960 of about 2 per cent as compared with 1959.

subtopic: AVAILABILITY OF EMPLOYMENT RECORDS OF UNEMPLOYED PERSONS
speechtext: What does all this show?

subtopic: AVAILABILITY OF EMPLOYMENT RECORDS OF UNEMPLOYED PERSONS
speechtext:
All this goes to show that unless we get the kind of expansion in the economy about which I have been talking, then the economy is not likely to pick up in the way it should pick up to take care of this unemployment. The report which we got from the Minister of Trade and Commerce this afternoon does not give us very much ground for hope in that regard. Indeed, the reports for the last three quarters of 1960 indicated a decline in most of the significant indices of economic activity, including general industrial production even though the minister, early in 1960, claimed the recession was over.
The fact is, Mr. Chairman, that the annual increase in our gross national product in real terms from 1950 to 1956, inclusive, on an average, was 5.6 per cent but from 1957 to 1959 the increase was 1.3 per cent. Unemployment, as a percentage of the labour force during the same period rose from 3.4 per cent on an average to 6.2 per cent. This tells the story of what has been happening to our economy in the last three or four years. It reflects a slowing down of that economy, a pause or recession, call it what you like. The governor of the Bank of Canada and the President of the United States are willing to use this word "recession", but this government will not use it. I ask the government and the minister, in the light of what I have just said and the evidence I have brought forward, if they feel that this recession is likely to continue further in 1961 or is it likely to recede? If it is likely to continue and our unemployment problem is likely to be with us, what are they doing about it in any effective way?
What is the outcome in respect of economic growth and resulting employment? Will the minister tell us that before this discussion is over? So far the minister has left us completely in the dark. Yet we know he receives two reports each year from a branch
Supply-Labour
of his department-the economics and research branch-the work of which he rightly praised this afternoon as being important and efficiently done. Now that we no longer have the report from the Department of Trade and Commerce-it is not only hidden but buried-perhaps the Minister of Labour could give us some information concerning what the experts of his department are telling him about the situation, the conclusions which he draws from that information and the plans he has as a result of those conclusions, if any. Perhaps he would also tell us how the plans to which he referred this afternoon are working out.
All we learned from the minister this afternoon is that President Kennedy is copying them; the plans which were put forward by this government in the autumn of 1960, three years after this unemployment problem hit this country. President Kennedy, not more than two or three weeks after his administration came to office, is carrying out plans which it took this government three years to put into operation here. On the face of it, that comparison does not make any sense. But even if the comparison were accurate, President Kennedy put his plans into effect two or three weeks after his election though it took hon. gentlemen opposite more than three years to do so. They took so long, it is obvious, because for three years they refused to admit there was any problem. When they took an attitude of that kind how could one expect them to adopt effective steps to deal with the situation?
All one has to do to realize the absurdity of the comparison which the minister has made with action taken by President Kennedy is to examine the proposals put forward by the president, and particularly the statement he made a couple of weeks ago to the national industrial conference in Washington; to examine the programs he is submitting to the United States congress, and compare them with the so-called emergency program which this government put forward last November and December.
Take, for example, the question of areas where there is chronic unemployment, depressed areas or whatever you may wish to call them; Mr. Kennedy is not afraid to call them depressed areas. Compare what he has done down there in three weeks, the action he has taken and the results which are already beginning to flow, with the statement we got from the minister the other day on the regulations which have been hanging fire for all these months to deal with areas of chronic unemployment here; regulations which have been well described by a paper which is traditionally a strong supporter of the government, the Globe and Mail. This is

Supply-Labour
what that newspaper had to say about them on March 6th. I read from an editorial: They constitute a poorly thought out and thoroughly inadequate approach to a serious problem. The old saying about a mountain labouring and bringing forth a mouse applies.
I do not think President Kennedy copied this particular kind of approach.
Now let me ask the minister if he will tell with regard to one effective and exciting program, as he referred to it this afternoon. He said something about winter works. Well, we expect to learn a lot more about the winter works program than we learned from his opening statement. The minister indicated that it had given employment to 200,000 people. Let the minister break down that figure and show us the nature of the employment provided to these 200,000 people. How many man hours does it cover? How many municipalities are concerned? What about the municipalities which have so much unemployment and are so poor in consequence that they cannot afford to take advantage of the government's program? What about the suggestion we have been making over the years that some special consideration should be given to those municipalities which need help most?
Will the minister tell us how many sewer projects have been started; how many students residences are now being built by the universities; how many loans have been made to small builders? These are all matters which have been put forward by the government as part of its answer to the question of unemployment. It is in our view an inadequate answer but if the minister is convinced that it is a good and effective answer, then perhaps he will give us more information instead of the present approach which is ineffective, hesitant, belated, piecemeal. This country in the face of 11 per cent or more unemployment needs something bold and imaginative, something worthy of the seriousness of the problem.
I tell the minister that this problem will never be solved in the way it should be solved and within the time during which it should be solved by the kind of approach which this government has been making. I refer the minister to the order in council which was tabled yesterday by the Minister of Trade and Commerce dealing with income tax regulations and the question of depreciation. That was dated March 3. When my hon. friend from Kenora-Rainy River on March 2, the day before this order in council was passed, did his very best to obtain from the Minister of Finance some indication of what was being done in this field he could get no information at all from the minister. Yet

the day after the Minister of Finance had refused to divulge that information, the order in council was passed giving all the details and it was tabled in this house yesterday. I do not know why we should have so much difficulty in getting information from the government about what it is doing in this important field unless the government has no information to give because it is not doing enough.
In Washington, where the new administration is tackling this problem with energy and vigour, they are worried whether they are doing enough. Professor Samuelson, a chief economic adviser to the President of the United States, said recently that an average rate of growth of 3J per cent to 4 per cent- and that is a modest rate of growth to take care of the increased labour force in this country-would have to wait until the second and third years of President Kennedy's term of office. This is another indication of how seriously they regard the situation south of the border.
Another United States economist, Dr. Heller, who is chairman of the council of economic advisers said to congress as reported in the New York Times of March 6 that:
Even if some success were encountered in improving the economic situation in the second and third quarters of 1961-
And we all hope that this success will be realized in terms of growth of the economy, and that the optimistic forecasts which are being made by some analysts will turn out to be right. I continue:
-much more serious in the long run is the "chronic slack" in employment production and the potential rate of growth-the growing gap between what we can produce and what we do produce.
Whenever it occurs the reversal of the recession is only the beginning, not the end, of the task of restoring momentum to the American economy.
If the ratio of unemployment to the total working force increases from the present 6.6 per cent to 7 per cent by the end of the year our fiscal policies would have to be viewed with great concern.
Here is the chief economic adviser to the United States government saying that if the unemployment ratio of the working force in his country goes up to 7 per cent, their whole fiscal policy will have to be viewed with great concern. He went on to explain what he meant by that, indicating that some pretty important and even drastic actions might have to be taken. The figure he mentioned is 7 per cent. The ratio of unemployment in this country today is 11 per cent, or it was almost 11 per cent in January.
Even making allowances for perhaps the exceptional seasonal character of employment in this country at that time, which they may not have in parts of the United States, our ratio of unemployment will still be above

the 7 per cent which the chief economic adviser to the United States government says requires drastic, effective fiscal action.
If that is true in the United States, it is even more true in this country because our situation-as I tried to show, Mr. Chairman- has certainly not been better, and indeed it has been more difficult, more complex and in some respects worse than the situation in the United States. It is deep-seated; it is deep-rooted; it is difficult, I know. It has expressed itself in this country in terms of 700,000 men and women being out of jobs in 1961, and it is time this government did something effective about it.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have listened with a great deal of interest to the frank admission of delinquency on the part of the Leader of the Opposition for that period of time when he and his colleagues were the government of this country. Surely to heavens, in view of the analysis that he has just given us, he should have been able to foresee these things when he sat on that side of the chamber. Perhaps if we had not had a moribund government at that time we would not have got into the difficulty that we are in today.
Supply-Labour
However, apart from that, the fact is that the opening remarks of the Minister of Labour were extremely disappointing. In view of the crisis that exists, in view of the things which we all hoped this government would be doing, to have a reference of perhaps two or three minutes duration on this particularly critical problem contained within remarks lasting for three quarters of an hour is, as I say, extremely disappointing.
The other parts of the minister's remarks about the expansion of the technical aspects of his department and its functions will undoubtedly be interesting and perhaps enlightening to a number of people, but they will not be of much help in this situation. The minister's department, so he has claimed, has in recent years been engaging in extensive research programs to assess what is existent within the economy, and to attempt to discover why the problem exists they have come up with all sorts of answers on different types of employment.
I do not recall them all offhand, but there are cyclical, seasonal, fractional and a variety of other descriptive words to classify types and reasons for unemployment. If this extensive research has been going on into the types and causes of unemployment, surely we could expect that the same sort of research would come up with some answers.
Perhaps they did come up with answers. Perhaps suggestions have been made and have been kept secret because the government did not wish to make them known to the public, thus indirectly admitting that there is a crisis existent in Canada today and that it has been in existence for a long period of time.
When there are no announcements of plans or programs in this regard, or for the reassessing of growth factors for the future, for this coming year and the following year, we can only come to the conclusion that the government has a barren and bankrupt mind on this particular problem.
The minister's comments in this regard were substantially the same as they were last year, the year before and the year before that. For all the time he has been Minister of Labour, including this year, the approach has been to gloss over the fact that there is a critical condition existing in the economy, and the government rests upon the hope that somebody else will be able to deal with it. "Let George do it", is obviously the attitude of this government.
I think this government fails to realize that the longer this crisis exists, the greater will be the destruction of the ability to work of individual, unemployed people. This is what existed during the depression years of the 1930's, when we also had a Tory government.

Supply-Labour
Long periods of unemployment in fact make psychological wrecks out of individuals who want to work more than anything else, who want to be employed, who want to do something constructive, who find regularly day after day after day that they are not accepted by society, they are not accepted by the economy, and the only place for them is in the soup kitchen or the breadline, begging for a hand-out or relying on welfare.
What does this do to the individual's ability to work? It wrecks, ruins and destroys it. It drives and forces that individual into a continual state of misery. This is what happens to individuals, apart from the fact that it is degrading enough not to have work. This is illustrated by the situation in Toronto, where children have to go, in effect, to soup kitchens for free meals because their parents obviously cannot find employment. I am referring to an account given in a newspaper that this is a situation which does exist.
