My hon. friend says, "Make sure you read all of it". If my hon. friend would read as much about this problem as I do, and exert as much of his energies as he should in urging that action be taken by his colleagues in the cabinet, perhaps we would not be discussing this serious problem at this time. If he and his comrades had the intestinal courage to face the fact that there is and has been unemployment year after year, perhaps this condition would not exist.
These unemployed individuals will come to look upon themselves as outcasts. The Minister of Labour knows this full well; he should know it, if he does not.
What are the psychological problems the individual must overcome after he has been unemployed for a long period of time? I feel that such an individual psychologically will not fit into the economic structure. This problem arose following the unemployment of the 1930's and accounts for the great number of derelicts in this country today. The existence of this type of individual following a period of unemployment is of little use to the general economy.
I feel that this government simply does not have the courage to admit the unemployment situation. It has not had that courage since it took office. The government has continued to ignore the situation by saying that to admit it would be to lose face. The government sits back with the hope that the economic forces, upon which the government and the Liberals rely, will heal the economic situation and everything will be rosy again. The minister and his colleagues have fiddled around with this problem like a modern day

Nero. There has been nothing done to deal with this problem in the way of concrete or lucid action. The taxpayers support inmates of penitentiaries to the extent of $5 a day while the government treats the unemployed workers of this nation as though they were members of an even lower class.
The minister refers to this exhilarating program including the productivity council, vocational training and double depreciation and the winter works projects, but they are merely ineffective first aid treatments for a very serious ailment and may be likened to treating a broken leg by the application of a band aid. The government has made no effort whatsoever to get to the basis of the problem. The minister speaks often of the incentive provided by the winter works program but admits by his actions in amending the program each year that it is not the cure-all it was supposed to be. He has brought this program forward again this year but suggests that if it is required next year it will be handled by supplementary estimate. He is in effect laying the groundwork for his answer to its failure.
I am sure that many individuals express the view that it is a waste of time for a member of parliament to stand here in this chamber urging the government to do something in respect of the unemployment situation. I am sure they feel that such an approach is an obvious waste of time in view of the government's blindness to the existing conditions. The government has done nothing to change this situation apart from putting into effect weak, ineffective measures such as those I have mentioned. I feel that we must persist in this approach in the hope that perhaps the government will take more effective action because one is alarmed by the fact that lives are being destroyed and children are without food because of the unemployment situation. Perhaps if we speak loud enough and long enough the minister and his colleagues will come to the conclusion that there is a problem and attempt to take steps to deal with it.
Mr. Chairman, my time is limited but I would like to mention two or three other specific items before I conclude. I am sure other hon. members will have an opportunity of dealing with the specific unemployment question from a philosophical base but I intend to limit my remarks to an attempt to convince the government that it has failed to deal with this question because of its political blindness regarding a society which is not working well, an economy that is not working well and a situation which needs a strong dose of socialist philosophy. I realize

that this suggestion is repugnant to the government even though it is actually the only effective one.
I should like to deal now with a question which the Leader of the Opposition briefly touched upon this afternoon namely, the functions of the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act. Last year the Leader of the Opposition quoted rather extensively from an article appearing in Saturday Night regarding a new approach to collective bargaining. Unfortunately I was not present in the house at that time when there was some discussion between the Minister of Labour and the Leader of the Opposition as to whether I was the author of the article. I belatedly admit that I was.

I thank the Leader of the Opposition for his remarks of that time regarding the substance of the article itself and must say that I also think it was a good article. It was my intention when writing that article to deal with a different approach to negotiations.
The Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act provides for the payment of the expenses of the chairman and members of a conciliation board. The act provides for the payment of $30 a day but authorizes the governor in council to increase this amount. It is my understanding that the payments exclusive of expenses have been in the neighbourhood of $50 to $75 per day. I feel that conciliation boards are a waste of time and certainly involve a waste of the taxpayers' money. When one takes into consideration the value a conciliation board contributes to the resolution of labour and the management difficulties one feels that the taxpayers' money might well be saved in this regard.
I have several orders in council with me today in which the name of Mr. David Lewis appears. I am now looking at one dated September, 1958 which indicates an allowance of $50 a day payable up to 16 days. I must indicate of course that it makes little difference to me whether it is Mr. Lewis receiving this money or someone else; I feel it is a waste of money. I feel the abolishing of these conciliation boards is a means of saving the taxpayers' money. I feel that conciliation boards are not beneficial in regard to industrial-management disputes. I feel the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act is outdated and has outlived its usefulness. The province of British Columbia has a similar labour act which outlines steps similar to those in the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act. There are differences between the two in regard to time

limits but substantially they outline the same steps in regard to negotiations, a conciliation officer and board, strikes, lockouts and perhaps subsequent negotiations.

As I said before, there are many people who think it is a complete waste of time to tell anything to a government that is deaf and blind to this particular problem, but I have made suggestions galore; specific, concrete proposals. They are all on Hansard. What happens? No interest is shown in them. They are there; they are still applicable.
My hon. friend may be interested in David Lewis and so on; maybe if this employment for David Lewis were cut off he might lose his income from conciliation activities. Nevertheless, I hope I am answering his specific question about proposals. They are on Hansard. I know how hon. gentlemen opposite dislike the truth, but it is there and if any hon. member wishes to read the numerous proposals I have made I will look through Hansard and pick out the positive suggestions which have been made, if that will do any good.
Let us get back to the conciliation board system. I am leading into industrial disputes and strikes. Unions and management have used the present system of negotiation toward the signing of collective agreements not for the purpose of bargaining in good faith-and I have used it myself, I am frank to admit- but for the purpose of delaying for one reason or another and wasting the time of the negotiating procedures either merely to get to the next step or in the hope that someone else will bail the two parties out of a difficult situation. This merely protracts and delays and takes them into a strike situation which is not too helpful.
But, in any event, the minister dealt briefly with this and, as I understood him, dealt with the accusation of the shifting of the responsibility which was levelled against him by the hon. member for Essex East. I think it is a shifting of responsibility if the minister says to those two groups, as he is prone to say to almost everybody else, "Do it yourself; get

Supply-Labour
yourself out of this difficult situation". This is not only a shifting of responsibility, it is an abandonment of responsibility, just as it is an abandonment of responsibility for the government to do nothing concrete about the unemployment situation.
Certainly if there were any sort of sensible approach to labour negotiations within the Department of Labour we undoubtedly would not be in the awkward position we are today, and the major railway unions and the railways might not be in the awkward position they are today. They were put there by this government merely because it abandoned or did not recognize its own responsibility in this field.
If the previous announcement means anything we are, I suppose, to have amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act. I should like to deal with the question of unemployment insurance for fishermen which is of prime importance to me not only because I have many fishermen in my constituency but by force of interest also. Mr. Chairman, in this debate that has been stirred up on the employment problem in Canada, I should like to attempt to bring out some of the underlying causes of the present uneasiness. In doing so, I shall stick to the facts as closely as possible in the firm belief that it is the only way to make a useful contribution to this type of discussion.

I shall not follow the example of certain members of the opposition in their demagogic efforts to please the electorate, especially the members for Essex East (Mr. Martin) and for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier). Those two members, deprived of their official prompter, would be hard put to state sound scientific arguments in the field of economics. I admit that this prompter, Mr. Maurice Lamontagne, enjoyed a good reputation at the time he was my teacher. Unfortunately, since he specialized in the writing of election pamphlets, he has lost track of economic realities.
Before starting my speech proper, I should like to denounce the blindness of all those who to better condemn the government define the present uneasiness solely in Canadian terms. This is either an outrageous aberration or a monstrous piece of dishonesty. The present unemployment is a problem throughout North America and the petty politicians who pretend to overlook this fact for vile partisan purposes, deserve to be denounced.
Only yesterday I read in the paper that the number of unemployed in the United States increased by 320,000 in February and reached 5,075,000, which is a record for the last 20 years. I read also that the 320,000 increase in February is three times the expected figure of 100,000. I only quote these figures, Mr. Chairman, to show the unfairness of these would-be politicians who, in a partisan spirit, have deliberately distorted the purpose of this debate.
A feature of the immediate aftermath of the war was the extraordinary development of private investment in Canada. This was only normal, since many big projects had been put off during the second world war. To illustrate this point, an economist mentioned the nearly complete dieselization of the railway systems in 1956 and 1957.
Industry as a whole had to make a huge effort in order to renew their plant and equipment.
There was new expansion of house building, which had been neglected for the sake of other industries of greater importance to our war effort.
There was a heavy demand for new houses, and thousands more were in urgent need of repairs. Canada turned to new production, to satisfy the demand from countries whose industrial equipment had been destroyed by war. This process has been excellently described by the president of the Montreal City 90205-6-1791
Supply-Labour
and District Savings Bank, Mr. Guy Vanier, who stated in its 114th annual report:
The ravages of war and the destruction of its means of production had made Europe dependent upon America. Owing to the tremendous accumulated demand, Canada was able to find outlets for all its products. That was an exceptional opportunity for a country with a great variety of raw materials but whose productive capacity was not yet up to the desirable level of development.
And yet, in spite of its material losses, Europe was not without any resources. Its population is traditionally given to hard work, and has always been renowned for technical know-how of the highest calibre. Thanks to the liberality of the United States, the countries of Europe found themselves with a considerable buying power in the very midst of all their trials, and they systematically reconstructed their plants. Nowhere in the world today can better equipment be found: because of the skill of their workers, and the lower wages paid, those countries have not only become largely self-sufficient but have been able to take over markets which we had temporarily made our own. Instead of warring between themselves and weakening one another, the countries of Europe have grouped themselves into a Common Market with the result that today Europe is the most powerful industrial unit after the United States.
It is obvious, Mr. Chairman, that artificial post-war conditions have created an equally artificial prosperity. We are justified to-day in blaming those who were then governing the country, who let themselves be blinded by a spurious prosperity and, either through ignorance or laziness, failed to take the necessary steps for an adjustment.
The lack of care and of foresight shown by the former Liberal administration is largely responsible for our present difficulties. So much for private investment.
Let us now turn to the many problems created by what is known as automation, the bitter effects of which have been felt in recent years and constitute a major challenge for managers and businessmen at this time. To fail, as did our opponents, to take into consideration the many consequences of this new phenomenon is, to say the least, a sign of a lack of insight and of realism. The replacing of men by machines cannot be accomplished without shaking the whole economy. Studies published in Canadian Labour which, as everyone knows, is the official organ of the Canadian Labour Congress, reveal disturbing facts. I would like to quote a few of them.
According to these statistics a 25 per cent reduction in the number of railroad workers, that is 35,000 workers, has resulted from railway dieselization. By using jet planes, T.C.A. has been able to effect a considerable increase

Supply-Labour
in the capacity of its aircraft and a 300 per cent increase in their speed. When one aircraft does the work of three, the effect on air line employment is readily seen. In the iron mining industry, production per man has gone up 250 per cent between 1952 and 1959, because of automation. From 1948 to 1958, the number of smelter workers has dropped 22.1 per cent but the output has risen 50 per cent while the value of production has almost doubled.
Let me quote a few other figures concerning the lumber industry, which I have found in a recent publication by the Canadian Pulp and Paper Association. The lumberman's average daily production has increased 38 per cent in the last decade due to improved equipment. If you take into consideration the total number of on-site workers the increase is 40 per cent.
According to Mr. R. Dymond, director of the economics and research branch in the Department of Labour, production increased 49.8 per cent in the car industry between 1949 and 1959. In the same period, the number of jobs available went up only 11 per cent. In the automobile parts industry, during the same period, production rose 19.7 per cent and the number of jobs available, only 6.8 per cent. In the electrical appliances industry, for the same period, production rose by 81.6 per cent, as compared to a 40.6 per cent increase in the number of jobs available. In the machine industry, the increase was 33.7 per cent in production and 16.8 per cent in the number of jobs. In the home appliances industry, it was 53.7 per cent in production and 19.3 per cent in the number of jobs. Those figures alone significantly demonstrate the effects of automation on unemployment.
The statistics I have just mentioned do not mean that I wish to over-simplify the problems created by technological developments and the introduction of modern mechanical, electrical and electronic devices. I do not want to dispute the fact that the development of improved means of production can, in general terms, represent a blessing for our economy. But it can never be too strongly emphasized that, over a short period, accelerated automation such as we have seen in recent years creates upheavals from which workers are the first to suffer.
The long term object of automation is increased output. It is a most desirable object for Canada whose main economic problem is to reduce the cost of production
[Mr. Morlssette.l
in order to successfully compete with foreign countries on the national and international markets. However short term policies must be adopted right now to protect workers displaced by machines.
May I insist on the fact that, in a country such as Canada, which is importing a large proportion of the new machines and new equipment, automation might well have particularly nefarious consequences for the workers. I like to think that the new productivity council will attach special importance to this problem. Problems of productivity cannot be divorced from those of the workers.
I see in the act providing for the establishment of a national productivity council that one of the objects of the council will be:
-to foster and promote the maintenance of good human relations in industry, the use of training programs at all levels of industry, the use of retraining programs to meet changing manpower requirements.
When it has discharged those necessary duties, the productivity council which, when it was established, was so violently criticized by our opponents, will have been of outstanding service to the country's economy.
I should like now to continue with what I would describe as a brief social study of unemployed manpower. To properly understand the problem of low employment, it is necessary to break down the total figure of unemployment into its main components. For instance, how can we not be deeply impressed by the fact that about 20 per cent of the jobless are young people still in their teens? In fact, out of the 429,000 unemployed registered in November, about 80,000 are from 14 to 19 years old. Out of 100 young people leaving school before they are 20 years old, 10 per cent and more are unemployed the year round. I refer to the November figures but, relatively speaking, the problem remains the same throughout the year. The problem is becoming more and more important, while it may be explained by the fact that there are a greater number of young people in Canada, as a result of the higher birth rate about 15 or 20 years ago.
Young people of 15 to 19 years old today were bom during the war when the birth rate was increasing. There were 60 per cent more births in the first five years following the war than during the five previous years. A great part of that surplus population is now overcrowding the labour market. I have given a few examples in connection with the number of unemployed among young people of

less than 20 years old. We now see that the number of workers among young people of 14 to 19 years old, reached 593,000 on January 14.
Therefore, it is obvious that the labour market is prematurely overcrowded by thousands of young people who could more usefully prepare themselves for the tasks of life by attending school, because education, as was indicated to the Senate committee on labour and employment, is directly related to unemployment.
In February 1960, the dominion bureau of statistics made a special survey of the education level of the unemployed. The results were simply astonishing. Among those who had not completed their primary studies, the proportion of unemployed was twice as high as among those who had completed them. It was six times higher than among those who had been through high school.
Statistics have shown also that the proportion of unemployed is much higher among non-specialized workers than among those who have a trade. In the light of those facts, it is easier to understand all the advantages which will result from the Technical and Vocational Training Assistance Act and from the setting up of the productivity council.
I referred a moment ago to the possible effects of automation. I should like to stress here that automation is being felt in agriculture perhaps more than anywhere else. The obvious result was a transfer of the labour force from the farming sector to the non-farming sector of the economy. In the last ten years, the number of farm workers has decreased by 340,000. In 1950, it reached a million and it was less than 700,000 in 1960. In other words, the non-farming sector had to absorb a supplementary labour force of
340,000	people.
Now, that transfer of farm labour is noticeable especially among young workers. Children of agricultural families, after less than elementary schooling, leave the land to seek jobs. The rate of transfer among young men and young girls of less than 20 years old is extraordinarily high. Among young people of 15 to 19 years old who were living on farms in 1951, two fifths had left the land in 1956. These young rural displaced workers, going to cities, generally belong to that category of workers who are more tragically affected by unemployment on account of their lack of education.
Supply-Labour
This is an alarming problem and it is extremely urgent that we take all means possible to provide these young people with the education, vocational and technical training that will allow them to find jobs more easily. That would offer a very wide field for the application of the technical and vocational training program undertaken by the federal government in co-operation with the provinces.
Economists are unanimous in forecasting that while the farm labour force, especially on account of automation, has substantially decreased, the same trend will continue in the next few years. In the last five years, the farm labour force has dropped by 150,000 workers; it is expected that it will lose some
70,000	more in the next five years. It has been estimated that employment in the non-agricultural sector will increase by 18 to 20 per cent from now until 1965.
Another important factor to note here, which might somewhat explain the present situation, is the fact that, in the last few years, the labour market has been invaded by a very great number of women. The rate of unemployment among women is less than half the rate for men. The female population has provided, these last few years, almost half the labour supply, but it has suffered much less than the male population from economic fluctuations. This is a relatively new sociological phenomenon, which those who analyse the employment situation should consider closely.
Mr. Chairman, I wanted to discuss briefly some of the problems resulting from the present employment situation in Canada. In describing these phenomena, I was able to show that their urgency and scope did not escape the government's attention. Ignoring the easy criticism and demagogy of political opponents who have been shamefully exploiting a serious problem and a difficult situation for election purposes, the federal government has adopted several long term policies, the advantages of which will certainly be felt in the future. I have mentioned more particularly the creation of the productivity council whose task it will be to try to solve the more basic problems in our economy. I have also referred to the legislation concerning technical and vocational training, which will also help to solve one of the most urgent problems of our times.
I shall not mention here all the legislation of more immediate application, which is also aimed at correcting the present situation.

Supply-Labour
The Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) has just announced that the winter works program promoted by the federal government in cooperation with the provincial governments has supplied direct work opportunities to about
100,000	people. There again, you have a policy which was violently critized by our opponents.
At the beginning of my remarks I pointed out that the slowdown in private investment is at the source of our present situation. When private investment slows down, it is the government's duty to provide assistance.
The Conservative government has had the courage to apply a contract-cyclical policy of budgetary deficit. Its public expense program has been quite impressive and has produced impressive results. Let me state only one example in that connection. Members will recall the extraordinary impetus given to the home construction industry in 1958 through the policy of the Conservative government. Again this year, extensive changes have been made to the National Housing Act and are about to produce more development in that industry.
The Minister of Public Works (Mr. Walker) announced in the house on March 1, 1961 that due to widening in the scope of the National Housing Act loan applications have reached a peak which was never equalled in Canadian history, except for a short period of a few weeks in 1958. Here is what the Minister of Public Works had to say:
Activity during the week of February 24, 1961 was extremely buoyant, with 1,205 requests for National Housing Act loans. This brought the total for the first eight weeks of the year to 7,381, compared with 650 in the same period last year. Of the 1961 total, the life insurance and trust and loan companies received 2,921 requests and Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation 4,460.
The Minister of Public Works pointed out that once the loans are converted into starts, employment opportunities will be provided for 35,000 men, and this is only for the first eight weeks of 1961.
I have tried, Mr. Chairman, in my remarks to the house, to bring out the effort made by this government to face up to the difficult situation we are going through at the moment and indeed to the problems confronting North American nations at the present time. I would like everybody to realize perfectly that the government did not bank on chance to solve the problems. It could not, under the circumstances, take advantage of certain developments like that of war and post-war. The

facts did not make ix good and easy for the government, as they did for the Liberal administration-
We should recall in this regard that in 1935, when the Liberals resumed power under misrepresentations, they were to restore Canada's economy and put an end to the serious unemployment of that time; we know that in 1939 they had done so little that the employment situation was worse that it has ever been recently as shown by the figures the Minister of Labour gave us recently. But war came to settle everything, if I may put it this way; after that came the post war period and the Korean war. It is only later that came to light some indication of the difficulties the government had to readjust our country's economy to peacetime conditions; those indications multiplied later to the extent that, in 1957, alarmed and concerned about the result of the oncoming elections, the Liberals had to hide from the public a report warning them to take immediate measures to check the rising recession.
This proves the Liberals have never been able to control a situation. Improvisers by profession and necessity, they showed themselves unable to realize the magnitude of those causes which were to subject our economy to the disturbances of which we are now aware. I cannot see how they could have authority now to play the busybodies. They place themselves quite imprudently in the situation of their swashbuckling former colleague, the present premier of Quebec; he also, as his former associates are boasting now, was to eliminate all trace of unemployment. All he did was to increase it. So, it will be up to the people, under the circumstances, to choose between sincere politicians and power thirsty demagogues.

Mr. Chairman, this afternoon, on the orders of the day, the Minister of Labour was asked a question by my hon. friend from Welland, the general purport of which was to this effect: could the minister, if any hon. member wished to have it, get the details of the application for employment of any person before the commission? The minister chose to identify this general question with that particular case about which he made a statement yesterday, and when he did that I made the charge that the minister in his statement of yesterday in answer to a question, which was not a spontaneous question and obviously had been planted by someone, was in breach of the law which was enacted by this parliament, namely section 98 of the Unemployment Insurance Act which reads as follows:

Information, written or verbal, obtained by the commission from any person pursuant to the provisions of this act or any regulation shall be made available only to the employees of the commission in the course of their employment and such other persons as the commission deems advisable-
The minister told us yesterday-and I will not trouble to read his statement unless anything I say is challenged; I have it here if it is-that the information he imparted to the house he obtained from the Hamilton office of the commission. He suggested that the officer who gave it to him was a person authorized to do so. I again draw your attention to the words "such other persons as the commission deems advisable". The act is quite specific about who is the commission. It reads:
There is hereby established a commission called the "unemployment insurance commission" consisting of three commissioners, appointed by the governor in council, of whom one shall be chief commissioner.
It is straining our credulity well beyond the breaking point, sir, to suggest for one minute that the commission met yesterday morning and that three commissioners, after due deliberation, particularly when one knows that the chief commissioner was not in Ottawa yesterday, decided that it was advisable to communicate this information to the minister for the purpose of making it public in contravention of the act.
Will the hon. member permit a question?

Not until I have concluded what I have to say and then I will only be too happy to answer the hon. gentleman's question because, knowing him, I know it will be a sensible one.
I am seeking to make an argument and it is, of course, a well-known device to try to prevent argument by asking questions, not that I am imputing an improper motive to the hon. gentleman. I want to go on and say that under the law this information is communicated to the commission which was set up as a body to be independent of the day to day administration of the government.
If parliament had wanted the Minister of Labour to administer the Unemployment Insurance Act parliament would have given that job to the Minister of Labour, but parliament in its wisdom saw fit to create a commission for that purpose precisely so that it would not be used for political and improper purposes. Parliament decided in its wisdom that this confidential information about people's private lives would be used only for the purpose of assisting them to

get jobs, not for the purpose of making political propaganda for any political party. I think, sir, in all my experience in parliament this is the most outrageous conduct I have ever seen on the part of any minister of the crown save one, and I shall have a word to say about that before I am through.
It so happens that yesterday also there was a motion on the order paper in the name of the hon. member for Assiniboia which was allowed to stand very shortly before the Minister of Labour made this outrageous statement. The hon. member for Assiniboia asked for certain correspondence regarding the discontinuance of the publication of statistical material relating to steel operating rates and steel producing capacity by the dominion bureau of statistics. What did the Minister of Trade and Commerce say about that? This is what he said:
Mr. Speaker, some doubts have been raised as to whether tabling of the information requested would be a violation of section 15 of the Statistics Act. Would the hon. member be agreeable to this motion standing until this point has been investigated?
Now, that was a very proper attitude to take, of course, and the hon. member properly allowed his motion to stand. But consider the difference between the two. The Minister of Trade and Commerce was afraid that he might give some information which would be prejudicial to two or three great producers of steel, great corporations in this country. On the other hand, the Minister of Labour, thinking he could smear a Canadian citizen who was out of work, and thereby discredit all Canadian citizens out of work, broke the law, defied the law made by parliament in order to make political propaganda,-
Nonsense.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
This afternoon the Leader of the Opposition asked the minister to comment on the manpower committee of the other place. Surely, he must know that it would be improper for the minister to make a statement on a committee sitting in the other place.
The Leader of the Opposition also made some reference to the unemployment insurance fund and to its depletion. Presumably, the unemployment insurance fund was established to assist people who were suffering from unemployment. This fund is bound to suffer depletion in a period when there is high unemployment. The opposition speaks from both sides of its mouth at once. It criticizes us for spending money out of the fund. Which way are they going to have it, Mr. Chairman? They cannot have it both ways.
The Leader of the Opposition also took exception to the Minister of Labour dealing with the affairs of this department. He apparently is not interested in such matters as vocational training, municipal winter works, civil rehabilitation and the other services provided by the department. If he were, he would have made some mention of them. He could hardly wait, Mr. Chairman, to give us a little lecture on the causes of unemployment. We are still waiting to hear about the cure, but I understand now that perhaps we will hear something from him later in this debate.
The Leader of the Opposition asked the minister about the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act, and wanted to know why it had not been amended. We are interested in hearing about the amendments he considers are necessary to this act. However, if he wants to know what the holdup is, I can tell him that labour and management have been so far apart in the amendments they have suggested it has not been possible to bring about any reconciliation in their respective views. One of the problems in this country may be that we have not been able to reconcile the views of management and labour. We are attempting to do so, Mr. Chairman, and we have called a meeting for that purpose for March 15 of this year.
The Leader of the Opposition spoke a great deal about President Kennedy. One would have almost thought President Kennedy was the new leader of the Liberal party, since the hon. member spoke in such glowing terms of him. I am not so sure President Kennedy would be prepared to accept such an honour.

However, I believe the reason why hon. members opposite do this is that what we have done to combat unemployment in all sectors stands out in shining contrast to their own dark and dismal record in this respect. They turn, therefore, to President Kennedy for a basis of comparison. Certainly this comparison is far more favourable than it would be if comparison were made with anything the Liberals had done.
I would point out, too, that President Kennedy is in the United States and we are in Canada. The Leader of the Opposition went to great lengths to quote the opinions of United States economists. This is quite all right and we do not take exception to it. However, I point out to him that the problem we have to solve is in this country and I would suggest that he turn his attention to what is happening here. I might add that we do not hesitate to compare our program with that presently being suggested by Kennedy. He is an energetic and aggressive young man with tremendous power at his disposal.
It is interesting in this connection to note that many of the things he is suggesting now are things that are already being done in this country or which are presently being introduced. Even the Leader of the Opposition will, I think, admit this. The other day President Kennedy said that labour and management must forget their differences and concentrate on areas of mutual interest. Apparently this statement has failed to come to the attention of the Leader of the Opposition.
On February 3, President Kennedy made certain proposals to congress. The Leader of the Opposition has invited an examination of those proposals and I hope he will not be disappointed by the results of that examination. TOiere were 12 matters. The first dealt with expansion in housing. This we brought about two years ago and we are still taking action in this field. He proposed an extension of the unemployment insurance benefit period to 39 weeks. It may surprise the Leader of the Opposition to learn that at the present time in Canada unemployment insurance benefits can be collected over a period of up to 77 weeks.
As far as the opposition are concerned I think they are just bankrupt of ideas and have tried to hide behind President Kennedy's success. We had a 40-minute economic analysis this afternoon but we did not have a minute for the cure. I commend the Leader of the Opposition on his analysis; I commend him for his bedside manner. But I cannot commend him for any prescription he had to offer.

duce a measure in this house we are met with cries from the opposition that it will not do any good. They fail to relate the whole package.
