speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
We are moving ahead, perhaps not at the rate all Canadians would like to see, and perhaps not at the rate that this government would like to see; but we are bringing in measures to deal with this situation and we shall continue to bring in measures which are suggested to this government as long as they are adaptable to the conditions which exist in this country.
May I say that the program of this government is the most massive program ever brought before a Canadian parliament to deal with the economic situation of this country. We are giving the type of leadership that is needed. I just mention in passing that my own university, Assumption University of Windsor, has an application before the central mortgage and housing corporation for a loan to make possible the construction of a new students' residence. That loan will be granted and it is another indication of what we are doing as a government to aid the economy of this country. It is also an example of what this government is doing to aid my own area, that is, the county of Essex.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext: The Leader of the Opposition will not like your talking that way.

There has been a good deal of comment about the ethics of the Minister of Labour in revealing the circumstances of Mr. Exelby who appeared on this now very famous C.B.C. program. I do not condone any person going on public television to portray in any way a situation which is not in accordance with the facts. If that has been done, the gentleman in question has made a mistake and the C.B.C. with him has made a mistake. But even if those mistakes have been made, in my opinion that does not justify the Minister of Labour standing up in the house to smear the person in question, to smear the C.B.C., but more important than that, to bring into question the situation affecting 693,000 unemployed persons in Canada.
It actually matters not to the unemployment situation in Canada whether or not this program was aired. The fact is that all over this nation there are tens of thousands of homes in which there is real suffering, in which there is heartache; and this government hides behind an error of one person, if in fact it was an error. The Minister of Labour, as has been said so well already, has himself broken the law and contravened the statute, but this is not the first time this method has been resorted to. After all, when a number of cards came to hon. members of this house there was evidence-
Mr. Chairman, will the hon. member permit a question?

-brought to our attention that some of the people who had signed the cards had been brought into the unemployment insurance offices and a great deal of pressure had been applied to them. They found that

the kind of gruelling they were given was not very pleasant. When the minister had this matter brought to his attention in the house he made some very tar-ranging and far-sweeping statements. He smeared well-known people in the labour movement that day, and when I asked him whether this matter would be referred to the industrial relations committee there was no reply.
It never sits. It has a chairman, but it does not sit.

I suggest that this question should be referred to the industrial relations committee. I suggest that we call before the committee the trade union people in question and these loose-tongued employees of the national employment service. Let us get to the facts; let us bring the minister before the committee and let us confront him with the evidence that has been brought to our attention.
Hear, hear.

This question is now more important than merely whether or not there has been some misrepresentation in certain matters. The present matter concerns whether or not confidential information in the hands of the government affecting the lives and happiness of Canadians may be disclosed at any time.
Surely our society has not reached the point where Canadians dare not give truthful and confidential information to government employees for fear that the minister may direct that this information be made available. In reply to this charge the parliamentary secretary said, "Look; we increased their salaries". I think that is entirely beside the point. Does an increase in salary mean that an employee, on instructions, must disclose information of a confidential character to be made public in the House of Commons?
Mr. Chairman, would the hon. member permit a question?

When I sit down I will permit all the questions you wish to ask. This summer we are going to have a census in our country. There will be information requested of every Canadian citizen. If the Minister of Labour will disclose confidential information, what guarantee is there that the Minister of Trade and Commerce will not disclose confidential information of this type for political advantage?
I say that Canadians are not safe in reporting information to the government or information in the census inquiry just so long as any member of this government may disclose information of a confidential character. Where is the bill of rights? Where is the protection to
Supply-Labour
ordinary Canadian citizens, when their private circumstances may be disclosed at any time by the Minister of Labour in the House of Commons and they have no opportunity to reply?
I suggest that this whole question regarding what took place at Galt should be brought before the industrial relations committee. Let us put on it the spotlight of a public inquiry, where one can hear the defence as well as the prosecution. The government's attitude to unemployment is apparently this. If the unemployment figures are high, they say, "We are making a massive attack to reduce unemployment and the main reason we cannot reduce it is because of what is said by the prophets of doom and gloom". Then they say, as a kind of last ditch argument, "Well, after all there are a lot of people who do not want to work. They have been forging names on cards. They have been offered employment, but they do not want to work".
How is it that so many Canadians became indolent and lazy during the time of this administration, when apparently there were so many less in this category a few years ago? If in 1956 the average unemployment was 200,000 persons, and we then heard no accusations that people were indolent, were sponging unemployment insurance and did not want to work, how is it that for last year the figure was up to 448,000? Does the minister say that 248,000 people are getting unemployment insurance in an illegal fashion?
We hear a great many excuses these days as to why there is so much unemployment. A few weeks ago the Minister of Finance said in this house that one of the reasons why there is so much trouble today with regard to unemployment is because of the wartime babies. He said there were too many wartime babies and they are now old enough to be on the labour market. He said, "We cannot deal with the love life of Canadians and the new citizens we have who are coming of working age. There were too many wartime babies". We asked why so many people are on the unemployment rolls. "Too many pregnant women drawing unemployment insurance who should not be receiving it". Some answer.
Everybody is responsible for the mess but the government, and it was this government that was going to clean up the mess; and there was a mess when the government came to office. The only trouble is that mess is bigger today and conditions are worse than they were before the government started this massive attack on unemployment.
The Minister of Labour and his parliamentary secretary apparently have the same scriptwriter. A lot of the same phraseology

Supply-Labour
appeared in the text of both statements. But they say that the government is on the job. The Minister of Labour said this afternoon, "We are constantly developing our understanding of unemployment and are obtaining a more effective utilization of our manpower resources through the work of the economics and research board".
There is more understanding and knowledge but less done with that understanding and knowledge, with more unemployment. Then the minister played an old record with an old theme. I heard the Minister of Labour speak to the Canadian Labour Congress delegation and thought he made a rather impressive speech. He outlined a lot of things that the government said it was doing but his conclusion bothered me. He said that the government had done its job and it is up to management and labour to carry on. We have asked him in the house if he has done anything to bring management and labour together; his answer was no. We have asked him in the house if he has made any recommendations to management and labour; his answer was no, the government has done all it is going to do and it is now up to management and labour.
The government said it wanted some ideas. It said it is making a massive attack on unemployment but would like more ideas. I can give the government more ideas. I mentioned over 25 points this afternoon which the Liberal party had suggested last year and most of them had to do with conferences bringing people together in talk fests. I can remember when the Prime Minister was in the opposition and every time the government made a mistake he suggested it call a conference-let us have another conference- and it had so many conferences that the leader of the opposition of that day became Prime Minister. We can have too many conferences. We need some action.
I would suggest that one of the things the government should do is change the financial policies of this country so that the interest rates are reduced. Just imagine that three quarters of a million Canadians are unemployed. The minister may say that they are indolent, he may say that they are lazy and do not want to work, he may say they are falsifying their evidence and making false statements on television but the statistical fact is that three quarters of a million people are unemployed and the provinces and municipalities are having to pay the highest interest rates they have paid in 20 years in floating their debentures.
We heard this evening that the main trouble is that the provinces are not doing their jobs. Let the government cut interest rates in half and the provinces will be able to

do a much more effective job than they can do when the government is choking provincial economies and choking provincial governments with this fantastically high rates of interest. I would suggest that this is the time for expansion in the money supply. This is not a time for tight money and high interest rates.
You are adopting our program.

I am not adopting your program at all. I am just saying that you were wrong when you were in government and the present government was wrong in opposition and that now they are just as wrong or perhaps worse in regard to interest rates than the Liberals were with their tight money policy. I would suggest that there should be a great national development program in which public money-the Liberals will never buy this one -should be invested in business and in industry. I would suggest that public money from the provinces be invested with federal moneys in a great national development program but the Liberals would not buy that program. That would be socialism and they do not want to have anything to do with socialism.
We will not even talk about it.
After all, they have got Joey Smallwood and the leader of the Liberal party in Saskatchewan so they will never adopt a great public investment program.
And you have got Tim Buck.

We are suggesting that this government should not be satisfied with embarking upon this one ribbon trans-Canada highway program that was started by the former administration. There should be a national highway program in this country and there should be public money invested in a main highway program in the provinces providing highways north and south. We suggest that the government should do something with the Clark report rather than allow it to sit on the shelf gathering dust.
The government is studying that report.

The government is not studying it. The government has not opened it since it received it, or at least the Minister of Labour has not. He does not have a clue as to what it contains and has not told the Prime Minister what is in it. Nothing is being done in regard to the Clark report. It is just gathering dust.
We believe that there is a need for a portable pension system in Canada. We feel

this is something that should be embarked on at this time. I have in my hand a report regarding the number of C.N.R. pensions being paid at various levels, which I received in reply to a question I asked in the house some days ago. This report indicates that there are 4,800 pensions being paid in the category of $100 or less. It indicates there are 2,708 individuals receiving a basic pension of $25 a month. This is an area where suffering exists. This is an area where purchasing power should be increased. We need a portable pension system, and that kind of system would not be a great financial drain on the public treasury. That type of pension system could be actuarially sound; money paid in during younger working years and taken out on retirement.

Mr. Chairman, on a point
of order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.
I thought you wanted some suggestions.

We are asking for some intelligent suggestions. We are discussing the labour estimates. My hon. friend, who is so loquacious, introduced the subject of portable pensions and national development programs. I am wondering if he is in order in doing so.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to speak to the point of order. The hon. member for Assiniboia has been outlining a program which in the main is a very acceptable one but it is a program of this party. The hon. member for Medicine Hat is now objecting to a contructive proposal being put forward. Surely that is not a point of order. I suggest that is the characteristic well-known effort of government members, interfering with constructive suggestions made in this house.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.
Mr. Chairman, may I speak to the point of order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think the hon. member for Assiniboia should speak to the point of order.

Mr. Chairman, I do not think that the Chair would rule that the discussion regarding a portable pension plan under item 1 of the Department of Labour estimates is not in order. However, the member for Essex East would have been more convincing had some of the hon. members of his party put forward suggestions in regard to these programs which he claims are those of his party.

We have been doing just that for over three years.
Supply-Labour

Mr. Chairman, when these people are in opposition they have a program but when they were in government they did not have a clue. There is no doubt that this proposal is in order, but if it were not then it would be in order in reply to the challenge of the Minister of Labour and his parliamentary secretary when they asked for ideas. We have many ideas, Mr. Chairman, and we are now trying to give them to the government. We believe that they are good ideas. I feel it is a disgrace to Canada to have over 2,000 persons on C.N.R. pensions at a base of $25 per month, 747 persons with a pension of between $25.01 and $29.99. Surely this is a disgrace to the nation, to the government and to the Prime Minister who said he was going to do something about these very low pensions.
I would also suggest that the old age pension in Canada should be increased. People who live on $55 a month and pay rent, are suffering from malnutrition. Let us increase the old age pension to $75 a month. Our old people will not put the increase in a jam can, stick it under the bed and leave it there. They will go out and spend it, and they will buy some of the goods that could be produced in some of our idle factories.
He's my boy.
I am glad the hon. member for Cariboo follows the practice of a former prime minister when he reached that age of accepting his cheque and cashing it.
I will.

He will, but I suggest to him something that is very obvious. Most people who reach the age of 70 years and receive a pension of $55 a month do not have a supplementary allowance paid out of the national treasury of anywhere near the size of the allowance that is received by the hon. member, and I get the same amount less the $55. I am not casting any reflection on the hon. member whom I consider a good friend and who sometimes makes a pertinent contribution to the debates in this house.
I suggest that at this time the government should endeavour to put purchasing power into the pockets of our agricultural producers. Export the wheat surplus and you will start the farm implement factories in this country operating once again. Export the surplus of Canadian grain and you will put some of the unemployed automobile workers back to work producing automobiles and trucks. There is a need for more consumption of goods in our country. Two thirds of the people of the world need more goods. In the 1940's Canada waged a very successful war effort in a time of national crisis. We never want to see another

Supply-Labour
fighting war, but I would suggest that now is the time for the government to declare war on unemployment and poverty in Canada and come to the assistance of underdeveloped countries by producing some of the goods that our idle factory workers would like to have the opportunity to produce.
Before I take my seat I should like to quote the words of a very famous Conservative, the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett, who had this to say in a radio broadcast in January, 1935:
X told you in 1931 I would end unemployment. That was a definite undertaking. By it I stand ... when I say I will correct the system, I mean that I will reform it. And when the system is reformed and in full operation again, there will be work for all. And in my mind, reform means government intervention. It means government control and regulation. It means the end of laissez faire. Reform heralds certain recovery.
I suggest that when the Prime Minister told the Canadian Labour Congress that come what may he was tied to the free enterprise system he admitted failure and until he starts putting into action these words which were given to the nation by a prime minister who was on his way out of office and which words were in fact a deathbed repentance, unemployment will be with us. We need a massive attack on unemployment. We submit the government has not yet started that attack.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit a question? He said he will accept questions at the conclusion of his speech. May I ask him now to give the page reference in Hansard of his statement that the Minister of Finance said that there were too many wartime babies?

The Minister of Finance did not say that. I can look it up and if the minister will give me a few minutes I will be glad to do it, and I shall quote it to him. The Minister of Finance said that one of the reasons the government was having a difficult time achieving a full employment economy was the high birth rate during the war. If the hon. gentleman will read the remarks carefully he will find this in the speech.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
On a point of order, I have the remarks in front of me. They appear on page 1001 of Hansard, at the bottom of the first column. The Minister of Finance made this statement:
However, the growth of our labour force is now more directly attributable to the coming of age, from an employment point of view at least, of the large number of babies who were born in Canada during and immediately after the war.
He said nothing about there being too many wartime babies. The hon. member for As-siniboia was quite incorrect in his statement.
No. He said that this was the reason unemployment was so high and he could not do anything about it.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: He said nothing about the problem being so big at all. There is nothing there relating to the problem of unemployment.
Except there were too many people coming of employment age and the government could not do anything about employment.

Is the hon. member's description of the statement made by the Minister of Labour this afternoon in connection with Mr. Exelby based on a completely erroneous interpretation of the law by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate or did he himself come to that conclusion on his own?
It is based on my own knowledge of public statutes and on a long experience in the House of Commons, much longer than that of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate.
Will the hon. member permit a further question? Does he think that we should look to Saskatchewan for proof that it is desirable for the government to go into competition with private business?
I think the Saskatchewan government has made a wonderful success of its crown corporations.
Oh, oh.

All that I know of. The Conservative party and the Liberal party in the province say, "If we get elected to office we will not touch them, we will leave them alone". They have been paying a return on investment in excess of 10 per cent, and my hon. friend from Greenwood would agree that that is a reasonable and satisfactory return.

Mr. Chairman, I am very pleased to be given this opportunity to take part in the debate on the estimates of the Department of Labour. My interest in this debate is precipitated by the remarks of some hon. members in the opposition, who state that our serious unemployment situation is unbearable in this country. But let me say right at the start that I am not minimizing the unemployment situation, far from it. I am just as much concerned as anybody else. Not one of us in the house enjoys the thought of men and women able and willing to work and unable to find it. At the same time, the cause of the unemployed people is not going to be helped when the impression is given in the country of a collapsing economy and blue ruin is shouted both here and abroad. Such far fetched distortions of gloom and doom undermine public confidence in our country and abroad.

To substantiate what I have just said let me give the committee an example. The other day I read a story in the Carillon News, Stein-bach, Manitoba, of Friday, February 10, 1961, about a grateful refugee lady from Russia who secured permission to leave Russia just about two or three weeks ago after trying unsuccessfully for about 15 years. This story went on to say that she was on her way to Vancouver when she met another lady on the plane "Britannia", which took her to her destination. This lady from Steinbach, Manitoba, was able to speak her own language and conversation ensued. The refugee lady told the Steinbach lady her life story and how it came about that she was now in Canada.
But this is not what I wanted to tell you, Mr. Chairman. What struck me most in this story was what the refugee lady from Russia had heard about Canada while still in Russia. She told the Steinbach lady that she had heard so much propaganda about the terrible unemployment in Canada that she was astonished and amazed at the evidence of prosperity everywhere in Canada. She was particularly struck by the difference between the Russian plane that brought her to Amsterdam and the Canadian plane that brought her the rest of the way, and was particularly pleased with the good food and excellent service on the Canadian plane. She said that everything looked so nice and clean and tidy in Canada in comparison with Moscow.
This story from Russia about the terrible unemployment in Canada comes from a country where the people have very little chance to get the real facts about Canada. They have no opportunity of reading our Canadian newspapers or magazines or of visiting our country to see for themselves the terrible unemployment in Canada. This one-sided propaganda emanating from Russia can certainly give an untrue picture of Canada to the Russian people in their homeland.
But, Mr. Chairman, this story about our terrible unemployment not only comes out of Russia. One can hear similar stories that emanate from other foreign countries about our terrible unemployment. Our own Prime Minister while visiting Ireland on his way to the conference in London was asked whether it was true that Canada's unemployment situation was so terribly serious. Yes, you can read these stories in our own press and you can hear them from the mouths of our own people, some of them, I must say, in very responsible positions. And, above all, you can hear about our terrible unemployment in the House of Commons of Canada.
We are all aware of our seasonal unemployment situation. We know there are more
Supply-Labour
Canadians out of work than any of us like to see and it is entirely proper that we should know about the situation and the reason for it. On the other hand, let us keep the record straight. How many Canadians, for instance, know that there is a labour force of 6,396,000 now in Canada, the highest in our history? It is 3.1 per cent higher than a year ago. How many know that in the last five years alone 800,000 people have been added to the working force? So much has been said about the rise of 165,000 in unemployed in January of this year but has anybody said that the employment figure in January was 47,000 higher than a year earlier? Has anybody said that 250,000 more Canadians have jobs today than at the same time three years ago or that more than 70 per cent of those without jobs have been unemployed less than three months, or that 60 per cent of the jobless come from families where one or more persons are still working?
Who would seriously deny the fact that there is much less hardship in being temporarily out of a job in these days of unemployment insurance than was the case 25 years ago? I can speak from personal experience because during the winter months at that time I had to work for board only and had to take care of my family at the same time. I am not citing these figures and facts in order to minimize the problem but they are relevant and significant facts and figures and they do make nonsense of the grossly misleading comparisons being made with the dirty 30's.
So, then, let us be clear on this point. If it is a serious problem, let us do something about it. Let us not only point a finger at the federal government and claim that unemployment is solely its responsibility and that the federal government should employ all those who are out of work. Let me tell you, Mr. Chairman, that all governments combined, federal, provincial and municipal, can only provide a very small portion of the jobs needed to keep our people employed. The great majority of jobs must be provided by industry engaged in the production of products that people will buy.
We must also realize that if we are to continue to have high employment in Canada we can only do so by industry producing products which will be competitive and will sell against competition. This is something which is clearly understood by the peoples of European and Asian countries and this is the reason why these countries are today our toughest competitors. If you ask them how they are able to do this, their answer is cooperation, co-operation between management and labour to bring about better design, higher quality and lower costs.

Supply-Labour
I must give them credit for that. These people are realists and they have always known that if a product is not competitive it will not sell and people will not be employed producing it. It is evident that such a result is not brought about by chance but by a planned effort by management and labour. Both these groups realize that by working separately they can accomplish very little whereas by working together they can accomplish a great deal. These countries are setting us an example which we would do well to adopt here in Canada.
Yes, Mr. Chairman, I believe that this co-operation can only be brought about by heads of companies inviting union representatives to study what is needed to increase sales, to make products more competitive and to work out co-operative plans to bring about increases in sales. If this co-operative planning and production were not possible to achieve in the past, it is high time that management and union leaders got together now. In an industrial world that is more competitive every day management, labour and government must work together as a team and, as a team, they can accomplish much.
Yes, Mr. Chairman, to provide employment we must produce goods either of better quality at the same price or of equal quality at a lower price than our competitors. Only then can we export our Canadian goods abroad and also sell Canadian-made goods in the home market at competitive prices. If we cannot compete effectively in export markets and if we cannot cope successfully with growing competition from imports in our own domestic markets, then I must say most regretfully that unemployment will stay with us for a long time.
Let us wake up to these facts and let us remember that the world does not owe us a living. We have to mould our own destiny and the sooner we realize this the better off we will be. Let us also remind ourselves that Canadians in the past have withstood many trials and tribulations but only when they were united in their efforts to overcome hardship and disaster. Let us never forget this.
We Canadians should not fail now when unemployment conditions are unavoidable and the government, with the best intentions in the world, cannot correct the situation immediately and consequently must rely on long range legislation to alleviate the unemployment situation.
The question is being asked, what is the government doing to help create work and combat unemployment? The answer to this, I would say, is that vigorous measures for combatting unemployment have already been implemented by the government. The winter works program is one. The Minister of Labour

described the response to the government winter works program for immediate employment as phenomenal in all respects, but he also said that he did not regard this type of work as the final cure for the economy or for the problem of unemployment.
This new Bill No. C-49, an act respecting technical and vocational training assistance to provinces, introduced by the minister, is another important piece of legislation. It has been heralded by many as a timely step taken by this government to increase technical training, combat unemployment and foster national development. Canada has never had sufficient trained manpower to meet the needs of industry. In the past, this country has relied on immigration to meet the need for trained manpower. The demand for skilled and technical workers is increasing far more rapidly than employment generally. The fastest growing occupations are those that require a high level of training. These are the occupations that are being pushed to the fore by rapid technological changes.
There are two kinds of training jobs to be done. First, we must train those already in the labour market who have left the regular school system, and are now unemployed, and second, we must provide more training for those now in school to ensure that the ranks of the unemployed will not be increased in the future. This bill indeed merits commendation. It provides for a program of education that could be characterized as a co-operative program with the provinces. It is designed for the immediate present and also for the future.
This government also introduced Bill No. C-52, an act for the establishment of a national productivity council. The Prime Minister made the suggestion at a conference on unemployment held in Ottawa in October last that a productivity council should be established. This specific proposal, which outlined the need for such a council and the function it might undertake, was accepted by leaders from commerce, industry, labour, finance and education. It has now become law and members of the council have already been appointed. In making this proposal, the Prime Minister stressed the need for full and active participation of Canadians in all sectors of the economy.
At a time when markets at home and abroad are becoming increasingly competitive, it is essential that Canadian industry be as efficient as possible. The national council should act as a policy making body and should assist in the establishment of regional and industrial productivity committees. In view of the progress made by other countries in the field of productivity, Canada cannot ignore this field of endeavour. As in other

countries where these councils have been so successfully used, Canada can achieve equally successful results if governments, management and labour co-operate fully to make Canadian products competitive in both quality and price.
Another thing that I should like to mention is the export trade promotion conference. Our trade commissioners from the 49 countries in which we have posts were called home so that they could advise our producers about the possibilities of selling their products in the various countries. Some 1,268 companies requested more than 10,500 interviews during the two-week period. It is too early to say what the conference accomplished, but we know that it enabled businessmen to gain information which it would have taken months of travel and an expenditure of thousands of dollars to acquire. It also convinced them that there is a market for their products abroad and that there is a far wider opportunity for selling their products in the countries of the world. These are some of the things the government is doing.
In conclusion, I should like to say that gloom should not pervade our spirits, even though we have many obstacles to overcome. With the co-operation of all governments, federal, provincial and municipal, as well as the people of our country, we should be able to overcome these temporary problems and build a better Canada for the benefit of all citizens of our country. Surely no one in this committee would deny the fact that this government, and in particular the Minister of Labour, is working toward this goal. If anyone questions this let him look at the minister's record over the last years and also at the record of this government since 1957.

Mr. Chairman, the debate this afternoon has been a most interesting one since it seems to have centred around a most peculiar point, that is the attempt by the Minister of Labour and those who sit on his side to take unto themselves the democratic President of the United States. There has been an attempt also by the hon. member for Assiniboia to take unto himself the mantle of the democrats in the United States. We in the Liberal party, Mr. Chairman, know with whom there has been a traditional alignment of the party to which the President of the United States belongs. I suggest to hon. members of this committee that they might consider the fact that hon. members opposite are led by a man whose name was not known and could not even be pronounced by the president prior to their first meeting.
This leader of the C.C.P. who, it seems, stands again for socialism, although the party to which he has long adhered has already
Supply-Labour
expired-a party which has had to deny socialism in order to elect the most intelligent and interesting young member from Peterborough-
They are going steady now.
His face is pink.

His face shows the colour to which he should properly adhere, the colour of all true radicals, namely red.
I consider, Mr. Chairman, that in debating the first item of the minister's estimates we should concern ourselves with what has been happening in Canada and not with the minister's attempts to mislead the people about what this government has been doing. He said this afternoon that unemployment is something which can be licked only by a massive attack. I suggest to hon. members of this committee that the sort of "no-cal diet" to which the government has been subjecting the people is not, by any definition, a massive attack.
Perhaps one indication of this massive attack is that panacea which was introduced last Friday by the Minister of Labour, double depreciation. The Leader of the Opposition referred to an editorial which appeared in a newspaper not noted for its support of the official opposition in this house. Some good points are made in this editorial and, oddly enough, some of them were touched upon by the hon. member for Port Arthur, who occasionally makes a remark worth listening to. On Your Honour's right are the hon. members who traditionally represent big business. However, through their spokesman, the Minister of Labour, they have shown a most abysmal ignorance of any kind of business, large or small, by attempting to say that this part of their massive attack, double depreciation, will in any way assist areas which need assistance.
Perhaps one of the things that is necessary is for hon. members of this committee to come to some agreement on the definition of terms. In my few short months in this chamber I have found it incredible that there was no agreement as to the meaning of words. One of the rather astonishing things, of course, was the speech from the throne in which the Prime Minister, through the Queen's representative, very carefully escaped using the word "unemployment". He carefully avoided using this until such time as he appeared on a television program and not before this house. Suddenly he decided that unemployment had made itself felt in the land and it was time he took his head from whatever snow bank it was hiding until the

Supply-Labour
snow melted and the unemployment went away; and decided he had better at least acknowledge the word.
If hon. members opposite wish to say that they follow Kennedy I should like to draw their attention to an article which appeared in the New York Herald Tribune entitled: "Kennedy Spells it Out-and it Reads 'Recession'". There must be some things about which hon. members agree with the president of our good neighbours to the south but this apparently has not been one until they found he had the moral courage to come before the people and say: hold on, there is danger in the land; it must be dealt with now and over a continuing period.
I think that neither the Minister of Labour nor his colleagues on the front bench dared say there was trouble. I suggest that the Minister of Labour has a special responsibility to be candid with this house and with the country, to admit that there is a problem; it is also his responsibility, because of his ministry, once the problem begins, to initiate immediately not only short range but long term panaceas or answers, for it is his responsibility to look after the people of Canada. Well, when a minister is not permitted even to acknowledge that there is a problem perhaps it is small wonder that he cannot begin to do anything about it. But when he suggests that there has been a massive attack exemplified by this measure of double depreciation for one year, anyone who knows business knows that no industry can even find a site within a period of one year, much less amass its capital, survey the labour force which would be available and make its other necessary arrangements. Who would want to start a canning factory where the labour pool would be asparagus cutters?
Many matters must be taken into consideration before a new plant is constructed, and I suggest to the Minister of Labour that if he is really interested in using this gimmick it should not be limited to new plants entering an area which is already one of surplus labour but it should be allowed to be used, if it is worth anything, by plants which are already in that area but which have closed for one reason or another. In their modernization, in their capital expansion, in their assistance in a number of ways, real help could be given to a particular area which has suffered from chronic unemployment.
We have been worrying about words from time to time. We hear words such as "rolling readjustment" which have finally come to "a recession". We hear words such as "depressed area", "distressed area" and "area of surplus labour". It may be that men and women of good faith do not understand the same
fMiss LaMarsh.l
things by the same words, but I suggest to the government and particularly to the Minister of Labour that it is a simple thing to spell out exactly what is meant by an area which needs government assistance.
The Minister of Labour has only produced a gimmick which will be of assistance to areas which are so deflated, so flattened already, as almost to have passed out of existence as far as the general economy is concerned. There are in Canada a great many other areas which are in trouble, yet which are not so depressed or so distressed or so flattened as to entitle them to qualify under this niggardly definition, these niggardly criteria placed before us by the minister. Such areas in Canada cry out for assistance.
This problem is not a new one. The Leader of the Official Opposition gave figures this afternoon showing that there have been four recessions, each increasingly severe, from each of which we have made a poor recovery in the past five or six years. This is a problem which cannot be dealt with by nit-picking. Just a few years ago hon. gentlemen opposite were supposed to have a particular and sole advantage in dealing with this subject. Theirs was the vision, and I ask them now; where has it disappeared? The people of this country look to them because they made some of the most glowing promises ever made to an electorate; and they have sold out the people of this country. They have not attempted to deal with this problem in any way.
They have not attempted anything, but whatever attempts are made-and it may be they will be made by another administration which will take power at the next election- this problem is one which is going to take a long time to solve. First, one must acknowledge its existence, and, second, one must start to work on it, and I suggest that one of the greatest responsibilities of this government is to get down to a massive assault. This is a problem which it is said, probably arises from too many babies, and from my experience of hon. members of this house they have nothing against babies almost until the age of twenty one. This may be part of the reason, but there are a number of other factors represented by a number of studies, some undertaken in the United States and some undertaken through the sittings in the other place. This problem requires an attack from all sides and one which will be long drawn out. It requires the kind of attack, the kind of study, perhaps, first, which was made at the behest of the President of the United States, one which deals with a two-prong matter, short term and long term proposals.
Would the hon. lady permit a question?

I would be very pleased to at the conclusion of my remarks. The report which was made was one of great length and if the Minister of Labour has not seen it I shall be glad to lend him my own copy. He has been asking the house for ideas.
We are grateful to the hon. member for Assiniboia for putting forth Liberal ideas. We are grateful that he has finally seen the light after sitting in the house and listening to the hon. member for Essex East, the hon. member for Laurier and the Leader of the Opposition for a year, for two years, for three years, telling those hon. members who are sitting to the right of the chairman what should be done and hearing the answer that nothing is ever told you.
I should like to offer the Minister of Labour the report which was made for the President of the United States. This report deals with a great many things, beginning with the most immediate sort of aid to those who are unemployed. I have no means of knowing whether this television program was another divertissment or whether it was intended to be factual. Perhaps it is not even important enough to concern hon. members of this committee. The reason that lies behind it is one which causes disquiet to every Canadian, regardless of his political affiliation.
There are those in this country who are in need of food. They are not, we can all thank our Maker, in the ascendancy. I suggest this is because of certain measures which have been in force for longer than the four years for which this administration is responsible. They are the measures which have kept people from starvation. However, there are those who need food. In this country there are great surpluses of food. The Minister of Agriculture is always trying to give away these surpluses. I saw today that they were giving away some of the surplus to a very well respected young visitor from the minister's own province, who was here for education week.
We want to use our food, and particularly we want to use it for those who are in need. One of the proposals made was that food be made available, on a proper nutritional basis, to those who needed it. Another thing which is necessary is housing. Arrangements have been made in the United States with respect to long term mortgages, a reduction of interest rates and a number of measures which will put housing within the reach of those persons still employed.
There are page after page of proposals to assist in the reconstruction of industry, in its automation and in relocation of industry in the United States. One of the things which is possible in the United States is the direction of defence contracts. In the last few years
Supply-Labour
there have not been too many defence contracts coming into Canada. However, there are some. The Minister of Labour may remember promising at least one to my riding not long ago. That is another promise in regard to which he has yet to make good. This is a way in which certain areas that are suffering to some degree, particularly industries, can be assisted.
The government has available to it all the experts who can tell them what industries and what areas require a shot in the arm. Not only is the government in a position to do this, but it is its real responsibility. Too many hon. members opposite appear to think that to be elected once or twice is enough. They appear to think that in the achieving of office they have done all that is necessary. May I suggest to the Minister of Labour and his colleagues that it is necessary not just to achieve office but to do something once you have arrived there.
Ideas to deal with unemployment have been placed before this house. I have seen them and I have referred to them a number of times. Suggestions were made in this connection on March 3 and 4, 1960 by the hon. member for Essex East. Earlier this session, on December 19, as reported at page 953 of Hansard, the hon. member for Laurier detailed what was being done in other countries of the world, such as Belgium, Germany, Sweden and Great Britain. But the minister has not seen fit to adopt these ideas. Not only in this house, but across this country otherwise hon. members have been saying that there have been no positive suggestions from the opposition. I suggest that if the Minister of Labour is incapable of remembering from day to day what has been suggested, a collection will be taken up on this side of the committee and a list will be printed and placed before him daily so that he will not forget them.
In January of this year there was a great meeting in Ottawa the like of which it is not expected will be seen even this month. Here the people of Canada, through their representatives, put forward certain proposals. These proposals were of many kinds, dealing with many of the problems which lie before the Canadian people.
I had the honour to serve on one committee which dealt with some of the problems of unemployment. We passed a resolution which I realize hon. gentlemen opposite cannot have seen, since they are not liberally-minded Canadians. Therefore, I place on the record what the party I represent has declared it stands for in the matter of dealing with depressed areas.
It was said in that committee that a new Liberal government today would co-operate

Supply-Labour
with provinces and municipalities in providing tax incentives to encourage industries to locate in such depressed areas. It would see that more credit was available to business in these areas. It would help to finance power, transport and other basic economic developments. Through programs for urban and rural rehabilitation it would see that both credit for private business and money for public improvement was readily available. I commend these things to the Minister of Labour.
There was, in addition, a resolution to deal with accelerated depreciation, but of a kind not contemplated by this government. The resolution was to the effect that a new Liberal government today would use the proven types of accelerated depreciation in order to help all business firms, not just new ones locating in an area, that are eager to expand and to put in new equipment. Such enterprises would thus, at a time when they most need cash, be paying lower taxes than firms that stand still.
The Minister of Labour said both today and in a speech he made to the advertising and sales club in Montreal on February 22 last that things are being done by this government, and they are things which have been followed in the country to the south. I refer to a remark made by the Minister of Labour during the speech to which I have just referred when he pointed out that the measures now proposed by President Kennedy were gratifying to the government in that they followed pretty well along the lines of what it had been doing in dealing with a very similar set of problems.
I wonder whether the Minister of Labour can tell us at what time he or other hon. members of his government forwarded to the President of the United States the intelligence necessary for him to take over leadership in the United States and the free world with such dizzy speed. The Minister of Labour also told us in this and other speeches that it is only necessary to wait until the massive program of this government has had an opportunity to make itself felt on the body politic.
I say to the Minister of Labour that the country cannot stand any more of the effects of the last three years. If this government is not now prepared to be candid, to be frank and to make a real effort to get this country moving, there is the great possibility that when the people of Canada have the opportunity to say whether or not they are satisfied with this government it will be too late for those of us who have ideas and are prepared to put them into effect to do anything.
Call for an election.
An hon. member to my right says "Call for an election". I notice that this is the hon. member who has said on a number of occasions that he will not be standing when there is another election.
The question is, will he be sitting afterwards.
Even if he stands he will not sit.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

There are those of us, Mr. Chairman, of the official and effective opposition who will be standing but not to Your Honour's left following the next election.
That which has been done by the Minister of Labour is something rather shocking to this committee. The Leader of the Opposition today posed question after question to the Minister of Labour, who sat only a few feet from him, and the minister made perhaps the weakest statement ever heard in such a debate. He countered these questions today with an ordinary routine speech about an ordinary routine department with no sense of urgency and with no realization of crisis in the country. The Minister of Labour may be content in his job and prepared to accept that the underbrush is being cleared, and that the massive program is sufficient to restore Canada's unemployed to full employment, but those of us who sit on this side are not prepared to sit silently while nothing is being done. Whenever, over the years, anyone rose on this side of the house to speak of the increasing unemployment figures it was not for political advantage.
Oh, oh.

I call the hon. members' attention to the numbers of members present in the committee of the number there might possibly be, and to the advantage that they might take in this chamber. This situation is impressed upon us because the members of the government appear not to notice or to care what is happening in the country.
Where there is no vision the people perish.

The only answer given to the country by the government was that we are glooming and dooming. We heard this again this evening from the hon. member who preceded me. Mr. Chairman, if glooming and dooming would put Canadians back to work those of us in the opposition would stoop to it. If what the government is trying to indicate to the people of Canada is that we are attempting to make them afraid and uncertain, that is not correct. We speak here in this chamber to those who at least temporarily

have the responsibility of doing something about it. I suppose that next they will adopt the famous remark of another democrat, Franklin Delano Roosevelt, who said to his people in the thirties, "We have nothing to fear but fear itself".
I would hope that as yet the Canadian economy has not been allowed in the last four years to slip so far that it cannot be recovered. If it has then we have considerably more to fear than fear itself. Those hon. members who sit opposite have a responsibility to the people and a responsibility which will not wait. I would suggest that rather than hon. members on the front bench travelling throughout this country making speeches and suggesting that the success of that administration to the south may be laid only to the fact that it has adopted the program existing in Canada, they should be here in this committee dealing with this massive attack of which they have so often spoken. If this cannot be done-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member but her time has expired.

I was wondering if the hon. member's enthusiastic embrace of President Kennedy's administration referred to the 50 per cent tariff increase on bicycles about ten days ago, and if she does not find this a little inconsistent with some of the suggestions made by hon. members in the front benches?
It may be that it is part of this massive attack to which the hon. members on the opposite side have referred so often in this house.

I should like to ask the
Minister of Labour if it is true that a member of the national employment service took part in the television program about which he claims there has been so much complaint.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

No one has complained about the program and it is true that national employment service persons took part in this program. All I have done is attempt to give additional facts in order to keep the record straight.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order.
Progress reported.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
May I inquire what the business of the house is for tomorrow, and
Business of the House
perhaps the house leader would also indicate what is planned for Monday and Tuesday of next week.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, tomorrow by general agreement we will start with the debate on Bill No. C-71, an act respecting the civil service of Canada. I understand that there will only be two or three members speaking on that occasion. This bill will then go to a special committee to be studied there and then come back to the house to be studied in the committee of the whole. If it is agreeable to the house, and that debate is concluded in good time, we will follow it with the motion of the Minister of Finance to set up the special committee to consider that bill. We will then carry on with the estimates of the Department of Labour.
The forecast for next week, subject to change if unexpected circumstances require, is as follows. Monday will be private members' day. Tuesday we would like to consider item No. 2 on today's order paper, second reading of Bill No. C-51, an act to amend the Coastal Fisheries Protection Act, and then take item No. 9 on today's order paper which is my resolution dealing with the Army Benevolent Fund Act. The third item on Tuesday would be item No. 14 on today's order paper which is the motion in the name of the Minister of Agriculture, asking the standing committee on agriculture to inquire into the prices of farm machinery. Then, item No. 4 on Tuesday would be item No. 8 on today's order paper, the resolution in the name of the Minister of Labour dealing with the vocational rehabilitation of disabled persons.
On Wednesday we would commence with Bill No. C-73, to amend the Income Tax Act. Should that be completed, we would then follow with item No. 12 on today's order paper, the resolution in the name of the Minister of Agriculture dealing with agricultural development.
Thursday's business would be a continuation of the items that I have called for Wednesday. If they are finished the remainder of the time on Thursday and on Friday would be devoted to the estimates of the Department of Agriculture.
May I just make the record clear? Regardless of the completion of the business as outlined for Tuesday, would we start with the income tax amendments on Wednesday?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Yes.
It being four minutes past ten o'clock, the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
